articles.title: Nuclear test veterans speak to BBC about search for justice
articles.summary: Andy Burnham says veterans will get 'the full truth' as he confirmed plans for an investigation into the health legacy of Britain's Cold War-era atomic programme.
articles.body:
Nuclear test veterans and their relatives have reacted to the prime minister's announcement of an investigation into the health legacy of Britain's Cold War-era atomic programme.

Andy Burham said a panel will assess the potential impact of testing exercises in the 1950s and 1960s on troops, adding that the process will be treated with the "utmost seriousness".

The BBC heard reaction from veterans and their families as part of Newsnight's 'Nuclear Test Veterans: The Newsnight Special'.

The Ministry of Defence (MoD) has for decades denied it covered up the impact of radiation on troops ordered to carry out nuclear weapons tests.

You can watch the full Newsnight special on BBC Two or on BBC iPlayer .

articles.summary: Wide toe box shoes can alleviate pain and help to prevent bunions and cramped feet. Podiatrists recommend wide toe box shoes from Altra, Hoka and more.
articles.body: If the sides of your shoes rub against your big toe or pinky toe, they are not wide enough — which means it may be time to consider shoes with a wide toe box. “This type of shoe is created with a more natural foot shape that widens at the top of the shoe (known as the toe box),” says Dr. Alissa Kuizinas, a board-certified podiatrist in Boston. “This allows space for your toes to splay and spread, so they can bend and flex naturally as you walk.” Beyond being more comfortable, sneakers with a wide toe box have a variety of other benefits. “They allow for better balance and stability, reducing the risk of tripping or falling,” says Dr. Isaac Tabari, a board-certified foot and ankle doctor and owner of NYC Podiatry Center of Excellence. A roomy toe box lets toes splay naturally, a breathable mesh upper keeps feet cool while logging miles and a rubber outsole provides grip. Keen is another one of Tabari’s favorite wide toe box shoe brands. The brand makes hiking shoes, sandals and walking shoes for both men and women. This sneaker falls into that last category. The sole is curved from heel to toe to help propel you forward and the upper is reinforced in high-impact places for maximum durability. The removable footbed offers arch support, according to Keen. Birkenstock is known for its comfortable sandals, but all shoes from the brand tend to have a wider overall fit, including a roomy toe box. These unisex casual sneakers have that, as well as a contoured footbed made from cork and latex for a cushiony yet supportive feel, according to the brand. The upper is made from leather and the rubber sole has treads for traction on slippery surfaces. Hey Dude shoes are lightweight and have wide toe boxes. Materials: Whether you are looking for walking sneakers, running sneakers or hiking shoes with a wide toe box, you’ll want them to last as long as possible. If your toes are constantly pinched, you may notice some not-so-pleasant effects. Compressing your bones together regularly can lead to blisters, corns, calluses, bunions and hammertoes, says Kuizinas. That said, some people may benefit from this shoe style more than others. “Shoes with a wide toe box allow for better balance and stability, reducing the risk of tripping or falling,” says Tabari. articles.title: Quarter of home-schooled children in South East have SEND
articles.summary: Two Brighton families say they felt they had no choice but to home-educate.
articles.body:
At least a quarter of children who are home-educated in Kent, Surrey and Sussex have a special educational need or disability (SEND), data obtained by the BBC shows.

Families have told BBC South East they decided to home-educate their children after feeling it was "the only thing left to do" and received little support from schools and local authorities.

An education expert said school budgets made it difficult to provide specialist provision.

The Department for Education (DfE) said its reforms, backed by £4bn, would "ensure every child gets the right support in their local school".

Both Aiyshah's children have autism and pathological demand avoidance (PDA) and her son also has ADHD.

Aiyshah, who lives in Brighton, said that at first, her daughter Mia was a "perfect role model, top of the class in everything".

"But at home, it was a completely different story," she said. "It was just anger, meltdowns, tears, everything, just all the time."

Eventually at the beginning of Year 3, "everything just exploded" she said, and Mia could not continue going to school.

The family did consider other options to home-schooling at this point, but decided that her daughter was unable to manage in any school environment.

They ruled out a SEND school as Aiyshah believed it would not be able to cater to her daughter's high academic ability.

"We just said, look, it doesn't matter what school it is, it's the school system," Aiyshah added.

Dr Amelia Roberts, an associate professor at University College London (UCL) and the head of the psychology and human development department, said Covid lockdowns showed home-schooling "can be really effective for children," and offer a "more flexible and more personalised" alternative to mainstream.

However, she said its effectiveness depended on the resources available to the parents.

In terms of meeting SEND children's needs, "schools are often in a really difficult place" with budgets being "historically very, very low," said Roberts.

"It shouldn't have to be a struggle... to deliver that intervention," Roberts said.

"So I think there are lots of reasons why it feels as if there are gaps in provision, even though many schools do incredible work."

In Kent, 24% of home-educated children were identified as having SEND, with 18% in Medway, a Freedom of Information request shows.

In Surrey, 36% had an additional need, with 25% in West Sussex.

Brighton and Hove City Council (BHCC) and East Sussex County Council both said it was not possible to provide us with this data but did tell us that 30 out of 729 and 59 out of 1459 of their home-educated children respectively had an education, health and care plan (EHCP).

EHCPs set out a child's specific needs and the support needed, but parents say they are difficult to apply for and many children with special needs do not have one.

Erica - also in Brighton - took her son Barney, who has autism, out of mainstream education.

"We sort of found out by experimentation that the school environment just wasn't going to work for him," she said.

Rather than being solely home-educated Barney is defined as being educated otherwise than at school (EOTAS).

"I spend time with my child helping him read every day or working on apps in relation to maths, but it also means things like forest school, having various tutors and play therapists come and spend time with him or him joining cooperative groups," Erica explains.

EOTAS is often arranged and funded by the local authority, whereas parents who choose to home-educate their children take full responsibility including of the finances.

A child needs an EHCP to qualify for EOTAS, which Erica said was "like a full-time job" to apply for.

Aiyshah said she received very little support from the council with her daughter's additional needs.

"Everything was down to me. It was down to me to keep recording and reporting," she said, eventually successfully applying for an EHCP for Mia.

Brighton and Hove City Council (BHCC) said it would not be appropriate to comment on individual children but it would "always be committed to working with parents, carers, young people and our local school community and services to ensure every child has access to quality education in a supportive and appropriate environment and given the opportunity to thrive".

"We are confident our schools and additional specialist provision are excellent options for children," a spokesperson said.

Home education was "daunting" at first, but Aiyshah found support in parents' home-school and SEND groups in Brighton and Hove and said she is"really, really glad" with her decision to home-school them.

A DfE spokesperson said: "No parent should feel they have no choice but to home educate.

"Our once-in-a-generation reforms, backed by £4bn, will ensure every child gets the right support in their local school."

They said the investment would mean improved inclusion, "raising the number of specialists on the ground and rolling out comprehensive training for every teacher".

"This comes alongside £3.7bn to create 60,000 specialist places across the country and help drive our target of inclusion bases in every secondary school, so that more children can thrive in a school that's right for them and remain part of wider school life," they added.

articles.title: Yaokwa: ritual indígena de MT pode virar Patrimônio da Humanidade | G1
articles.standfirst: Celebração abre o calendário do povo Enawenê Nawê com uma pescaria feita com barragens tradicionais. A Unesco avalia a candidatura entre 30 de novembro e 5 de dezembro, em Xiamen.
articles.summary: O Ritual Yaokwa, celebração de sete meses do povo Enawenê Nawê em Mato Grosso, será avaliado pela Unesco para se tornar Patrimônio Cultural Imaterial da Humanidade.
articles.body:
Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

O Ritual Yaokwa , celebração de cerca de sete meses que marca o início do calendário anual do povo indígena Enawenê Nawê, em Mato Grosso, pode se tornar Patrimônio Cultural Imaterial da Humanidade . A candidatura será avaliada pelo comitê responsável pela proteção do patrimônio imaterial da Organização das Nações Unidas para a Educação, a Ciência e a Cultura (Unesco), que se reúne entre 30 de novembro e 5 de dezembro, em Xiamen, na China.

O ritual já tem reconhecimento da Unesco desde 2011, quando foi incluído na lista de bens culturais que precisam de medidas urgentes de proteção e se tornou o único bem cultural brasileiro nessa lista. Agora, a pedido dos próprios Enawenê Nawê, o comitê vai analisar a transferência para a Lista Representativa do Patrimônio Cultural Imaterial da Humanidade. O pedido reúne os resultados das ações desenvolvidas nos últimos 15 anos pelos indígenas, em parceria com o Instituto do Patrimônio Histórico e Artístico Nacional (Iphan) e outras instituições.

Na mesma sessão, a Unesco também vai avaliar a candidatura do Maracatu Nação, manifestação afro-brasileira da Região Metropolitana do Recife (PE) que reúne música, dança e espiritualidade.

Ritual Yaokwa do povo indígena Enawenê Nawê — Foto: Iphan

Também grafado como Yãkwa , o ritual começa no período da seca, quando os homens saem para a principal pescaria ritual do ano. Para capturar os peixes, eles constroem barragens com técnicas tradicionais. Ao longo de cerca de sete meses, a celebração mobiliza conhecimentos que vão da agricultura e da pesca à culinária e às práticas espirituais .

Para a principal pescaria ritual do ano, os Enawenê Nawê constroem barragens com técnicas tradicionais — Foto: Iphan

Os Enawenê Nawê vivem na bacia do Rio Juruena, no noroeste de Mato Grosso. Ao lado dos rituais Lerohi, Salomã e Kateoko, o Yaokwa organiza o calendário e a vida coletiva do povo, além de orientar a relação da comunidade com o território e o mundo espiritual.

A realização da celebração depende das condições ambientais da região, ameaçadas há décadas pelo desmatamento no entorno da terra indígena , por invasões ao território e pela construção de hidrelétricas na bacia do Juruena .

Até 2024, área desmatada na Terra Indígena Enawene Nawe equivalia a cerca de 4,5 mil campos de futebol, segundo o Instituto Socioambiental — Foto: Prefeitura de Juína

Se aprovada, a transferência para a Lista Representativa reforça o compromisso internacional com a proteção do ritual. A inclusão também pode dar impulso a políticas públicas e aproximar os Enawenê Nawê de redes internacionais de comunidades, mestres e especialistas que trabalham pela continuidade de práticas culturais.

articles.title: Tempo de Brincar: campanha de Natal quer arrecadar 10 mil brinquedos | G1
articles.standfirst: Iniciativa recebe brinquedos novos ou usados em bom estado para crianças de até 10 anos; campanha também terá drive-thru solidário em dezembro.
articles.summary: Iniciativa recebe brinquedos novos ou usados em bom estado para crianças de até 10 anos; campanha também terá drive-thru solidário em dezembro.
articles.body:
Campanha Natal - Tempo de Brincar tem mascote Naná — Foto: Divulgação

Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

Uma campanha solidária quer arrecadar 10 mil brinquedos para tornar o Natal de crianças mais feliz em Mato Grosso do Sul. A iniciativa Natal – Tempo de Brincar, realizada pela TV Morena em parceria com os Correios e com apoio do MS Cap, recebe doações de brinquedos novos ou usados em bom estado de conservação.

A campanha conta com mais de 20 pontos de arrecadação espalhados pela região. As doações podem ser entregues na TV Morena, na MS Cap e nas agências dos Correios participantes.

Podem ser doados brinquedos adequados para crianças de até 10 anos, como ursinhos de pelúcia, carrinhos, bonecas e jogos de tabuleiro.

Esta é a primeira edição da campanha, que também busca mobilizar a população e incentivar a solidariedade. A previsão é que os brinquedos sejam distribuídos antes do Natal.

Parte das doações será destinada a entidades que atendem crianças. Outra parte ajudará a campanha de Natal dos Correios, que busca presentear crianças que escreveram cartinhas, mas ainda não conseguiram padrinhos.

Para aproximar o público e incentivar a participação de famílias e crianças, a campanha tem uma personagem especial: a Naná, uma meia natalina que simboliza o espírito acolhedor da mobilização.

Guiada pelo lema "Quanto mais cheia eu fico, mais corações eu abraço!", a mascote representa a proposta de transformar cada doação em um gesto de carinho e solidariedade.

Brinquedos serão separados por faixa etária

Os brinquedos arrecadados nos pontos de coleta serão reunidos nas agências dos Correios. A triagem será realizada desde o início da campanha, para separar os itens de acordo com a faixa etária das crianças que receberão os presentes.

Além dos pontos fixos de arrecadação, a campanha terá uma mobilização especial chamada Dia N. Um drive-thru solidário será realizado em 19 de dezembro, das 8h às 12h.

A iniciativa permitirá que as pessoas entreguem os brinquedos sem precisar sair do carro. O local ainda será confirmado.

As doações nos pontos fixos podem ser feitas até 16 de dezembro.

articles.title: Falha em radar afeta mais de 300 voos nos Estados Unidos | G1
articles.standfirst: Problema impactou partidas e chegadas no Aeroporto de Chicago, um dos maiores do país. Falha acontece às vésperas do feriado de Ação de Graças.
articles.summary: Problema impactou partidas e chegadas no Aeroporto de Chicago, um dos maiores do país. Falha acontece às vésperas do feriado de Ação de Graças.
articles.body:
Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

Uma falha em um sistema de radar em solo está provocando atrasos em voos nos Estados Unidos , nesta terça-feira (24). Cerca de 370 voos registraram atrasos. Desse total, 214 tinham Chicago como destino.

O problema acontece às vésperas do feriado de Ação de Graças, um dos períodos de maior movimento nos aeroportos norte-americanos. Milhões de pessoas viajam pelo país para passar o feriado com familiares e amigos.

A falha está concentrada no Aeroporto Internacional O'Hare, em Chicago, e afeta um equipamento usado pelo controle de tráfego aéreo.

A ferramenta em questão é usada para monitorar aviões e veículos nas pistas e nas áreas de circulação do aeroporto.

Segundo as autoridades norte-americanas, técnicos trabalham para reparar o sistema.

O aeroporto de Chicago é um dos principais centros de operações das companhias American Airlines e United Airlines. Por isso, os atrasos também podem afetar passageiros que fazem conexões em Chicago para chegar a outros destinos nos Estados Unidos.

Segundo a Administração Federal de Aviação (FAA, na sigla em inglês), os atrasos eram, em média, de 47 minutos. A previsão era de que o problema continuasse até a madrugada de quarta-feira (25).

Ukrainian forces destroyed a Russian warship docked in the Libyan port of Benghazi and struck a cargo vessel just offshore.

The escalation risks dragging the oil-rich but politically divided North African nation – where Russia already has a presence – into the conflict.

articles.title: Colombia at a Crossroads: Searching for peace amid conflict
articles.summary: A decade after Colombia’s peace accords, former FARC fighter and artist honours killed signatories with a mural.
articles.body:
Yuheni Izquierdo, a former FARC fighter turned artist, paints a mural commemorating fellow peace signatories killed since Colombia’s 2016 Havana peace accords. More than 50 years of armed conflict formally ended with the agreement, but hundreds of signatories have since been killed as armed groups carry out reprisals and fight for territorial control.

Yuheni fears that the escalating violence threatens to return the country to a past that claimed more than 450,000 lives and hopes her mural will inspire Colombians to believe that a lasting peace is possible.

Colombia at a Crossroads is a documentary film by Rodrigo Vazquez Salessi.

articles.body:

A Agência Central de Inteligência (CIA, na sigla em inglês) e o Escritório do Diretor de Inteligência Nacional dos Estados Unidos identificaram uma invasão cibernética que expôs informações não sigilosas dos órgãos, segundo o jornal americano "The New York Times".

O ataque atingiu um sistema de análise de inteligência de fontes abertas, usado para identificar informações relevantes em materiais públicos e não classificados, disseram as fontes do gonverno dos EUA ao jornal.

➡️ É o segundo incidente envolvendo os sistemas de inteligência do país em menos de uma semana. Na terça-feira passada (17), a rede interna de comunicações da Agência de Segurança Nacional dos Estados Unidos (NSA, na sigla em inglês), usada para repassar informações altamente sigilosas, ficou fora do ar por dias.

Ainda não se sabe exatamente quais informações foram acessadas pelos invasores. Segundo as fontes, porém, dados sigilosos não foram comprometidos. Há suspeitas de que informações de outros órgãos do governo americano também tenham sido expostas.

Fontes ouvidas pelo NYT afirmam que os episódios aumentaram a preocupação de autoridades e ex-integrantes da comunidade de inteligência dos Estados Unidos. Segundo funcionários do governo, ferramentas de inteligência artificial estão identificando vulnerabilidades em programas de computador que precisam ser corrigidas rapidamente.

No caso da CIA e do Escritório do Diretor de Inteligência Nacional, há indícios de que um hacker tenha conseguido acessar sem autorização pelo menos um sistema do governo. As fontes não informaram se os investigadores identificaram o responsável pela invasão.

Na semana passada, o presidente Donald Trump confirmou que o Centro Nacional de Informações sobre Crimes do FBI, um banco de dados usado por órgãos policiais municipais, estaduais e federais para compartilhar informações sobre suspeitos de crimes, também havia sido invadido.

"Vou dizer que isso não é bom. Não gosto disso", afirmou Trump no sábado, em entrevista por telefone à emissora Fox News, ao ser questionado sobre o ataque.

O FBI investiga o caso, segundo as fontes.

Também na semana passada, o Departamento de Agricultura dos Estados Unidos identificou um incidente de segurança cibernética que levou à retirada do ar de alguns de seus aplicativos internos.

Os casos se somam a uma lista de falhas e ataques de sistemas públicos e privados do país. Apesar das questões tecnológicas, não há ligação aparente entre os episódios. Veja a lista :

Apagão na Microsoft : uma falha global nos serviços da Microsoft afetou empresas, governos e serviços de emergência em dezenas de países . O problema começou em 12 de novembro e persistiu até o dia seguinte, com falhas em ferramentas amplamente utilizadas no ambiente de trabalho, como o Outlook, o Teams e o assistente de inteligência artificial Copilot.

Apagão aéreo nos EUA : a paralisação de todos os aeroportos dos Estados Unidos , com pousos e decolagens interrompidos em 13 de novembro. Uma falha no sistema de comunicação dos controladores de voo fez o país bloquear por mais de quatro horas o tráfego aéreo.

Falhas com bancos : grandes bancos dos Estados Unidos registraram problemas na segunda-feira passada (16) . Milhares de clientes relataram dificuldades para acessar contas bancárias pela internet após um problema técnico em uma instituição financeira provocar um efeito cascata no sistema americano.

Problemas generalizados na United Airlines : também no último dia 16, a companhia aérea enfrentou uma falha em seus sistemas que provocou atrasos em alguns voos . Segundo a empresa, o problema foi resolvido em poucas horas. Após a solução, a companhia esclareceu que não havia indícios de ciberataque.

articles.title: A Welsh slate museum housed in historic quarry workshops closed in 2024 for a major renovation; a fresh £2.4 million government grant will help restore the UNESCO-listed industrial site and create new facilities
articles.summary: There are places where history is not simply preserved in books, photographs or museum displays, but remains embedded in the very buildings where it
articles.body: There are places where history is not simply preserved in books, photographs or museum displays, but remains embedded in the very buildings where it unfolded. Old workshops, factories and industrial sites often hold traces of an era when their machinery was part of everyday life, and the people who worked there helped shape the fortunes of entire regions. With time, however, the industries that once kept these places alive may disappear, leaving behind structures that offer a glimpse into the skills, labour and communities of an earlier age. Preserving them is not merely an exercise in restoring old buildings; it is also about ensuring that the stories associated with them are not lost.In north-west Wales, the National Slate Museum in Llanberis is one such place. Housed in the historic Gilfach Ddu workshops of the former Dinorwig quarry, the museum preserves the legacy of an industry that transformed the region and became an important part of its cultural identity. The site, which forms part of the UNESCO-listed Slate Landscape of Northwest Wales, closed to visitors in November 2024 for a major redevelopment. Now, a fresh £2.4 million investment from the Welsh Government is expected to support the restoration of its historic buildings and the creation of new facilities as the museum prepares for its eventual reopening.According to the Welsh Government's announcement, the funding will go towards the next phase of a wider redevelopment project being carried out by Amgueddfa Cymru – Museum Wales. Culture and Sport Cabinet Minister Heledd Fychan confirmed the additional investment during a visit to the site, highlighting the importance of preserving the historic workshops while making the museum more welcoming and accessible to future visitors. The project brings together conservation work and the development of new facilities, with the aim of giving the museum a sustainable future without compromising its industrial character.What the restoration work at the museum involvesA major part of the restoration involves bringing the historic workshops back to life while retaining the features that make them an important part of Wales' industrial heritage. The work is not simply about repairing an old building, but about preserving the details that have survived from the days when the workshops served the Dinorwig quarry. This includes the restoration of 113 original windows, which together contain almost 12,000 individual pieces of glass. Rather than replacing them altogether, specialists are carefully repairing the existing frames and glass panels wherever possible. The original wooden doors are also being restored, with damaged sections of timber repaired to retain their historic appearance.Alongside the conservation work, the redevelopment is also preparing the museum for a different kind of visitor experience. The plans include improved spaces and facilities that will allow people to explore the history of the slate industry while spending more time at the site. The challenge is to strike a balance between preserving a place that reflects a very different period of industrial life and making it suitable for visitors today. In that sense, the restoration is as much about protecting the museum's original character as it is about preparing it for the future.What new facilities visitors can expect after reopeningAmong the additions planned for the museum is a new café, learning and community centre, which will replace the older shop and café buildings that were demolished during the redevelopment. The new space will give visitors somewhere to spend time at the site, while also providing facilities for school visits, educational activities and local community events. A dedicated play area is also being developed for children, with elements inspired by the region's slate heritage. Along with improved exhibition spaces, these facilities are expected to make the museum more accessible to families and younger visitors, giving them an opportunity to learn about the industry beyond the machinery and objects on display.The National Slate Museum's redevelopment comes at a time when preserving industrial heritage has become an important part of keeping local histories alive. The slate industry may no longer define everyday life in north-west Wales as it once did, but its influence can still be seen across the region's landscape, architecture and communities. When the museum eventually reopens, visitors will find some new facilities, but the purpose of the place will remain much the same: to tell the story of the workers, their craft and an industry that helped shape an entire region. The additional funding is therefore not just an investment in a museum, but in keeping that history accessible to generations who may otherwise know little about it.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Texas mother with Alzheimer's left her home to her daughter in a 2007 will, but her son used a power of attorney to deed himself a share for $10; an appeals court ruled the transfer invalid
articles.summary: A family dispute over a Texas woman's home has ended with an appeals court upholding a ruling that invalidated a property transfer made by her son using a
articles.body: A family dispute over a Texas woman's home has ended with an appeals court upholding a ruling that invalidated a property transfer made by her son using a power of attorney. The mother, Betty Lou Casey, had left her Arlington residence to her daughter in a 2007 will. Years later, her son, Danny Prine, used a power of attorney purportedly granted by his mother to transfer the property to himself and her for a stated consideration of just $10. In an opinion filed on November 19, 2026, available on Justia, the Texas Eleventh Court of Appeals affirmed the probate court's decision, finding that Casey lacked the mental capacity to execute the power of attorney on which the transfer depended.A 2007 will left the Arlington home to the daughterCasey had three children: Sheila Fisher, Danny Prine and Sherry Neustupa. Her will, dated August 7, 2007, named Fisher as the independent executor of her estate and specifically left her Tarrant County residence on Milby Road in Arlington to her. The remainder of her estate was to be divided equally among the three children.Casey had also signed a durable power of attorney in 2007, naming Fisher as her agent. However, on November 21, 2014, she executed another power of attorney that designated Prine as her agent and Sherry as the alternative agent. Casey had been diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease in 2014. Her condition gradually deteriorated, and she died on November 13, 2021, aged 92.During the probate process, Fisher discovered that her brother had executed a warranty deed on February 5, 2021, using the 2014 power of attorney. The document purported to convey the Arlington property to Prine and Casey as joint tenants for a stated consideration of $10. The deed did not contain survivorship language. Prine later re-recorded the deed on July 14, 2022, after Fisher had demanded that he leave the property.Medical evidence raised questions about the power of attorneyFisher challenged the validity of the 2014 power of attorney and the subsequent property deed. She argued that their mother did not have the mental capacity to execute the document that authorised Prine to act on her behalf. During the trial, Casey's treating physician, Dr Joe Perryman III, testified that he had treated her from 2013 to 2020. She had been diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease and dementia in 2014 and was prescribed medications for cognitive decline. Her primary symptom was memory loss, and her condition progressively worsened.Casey's grandson also testified that he had noticed her memory problems as early as 2011. By 2014, she was increasingly confused, sometimes unable to remember what had happened the previous day, and could no longer manage her finances or prepare meals independently. Fisher described similar changes, saying their mother frequently forgot to pay bills, misplaced belongings and sometimes forgot to eat. She had also begun helping Casey with meals, shopping and medical appointments.An important part of the evidence came from Prine himself. On November 21, 2014, the same day Casey signed the power of attorney naming him as her agent, he had submitted a sworn statement in another estate matter describing his mother as incapacitated because of dementia and unable to manage her affairs. Although Prine later testified that Casey appeared lucid when she signed the document, the probate court found that she lacked the necessary mental capacity.Appeals court upholds the invalidation of the deedThe probate court ruled on March 6, 2025, that the 2014 power of attorney was invalid, the February 2021 deed was invalid, and full ownership of the Arlington property vested in Fisher immediately upon Casey's death. Prine challenged the decision, arguing that the evidence did not establish his mother's incapacity and that the court had wrongly invalidated the deed. He also raised complaints about his sister's handling of the estate.The appeals court rejected his arguments. It explained that the evidence was sufficient to support the finding that Casey did not understand the nature and consequences of signing the 2014 power of attorney. It also noted that Prine's own sworn statement about her incapacity, made on the very day she signed the document, supported that conclusion.The court further explained that a transaction in which an agent transfers property to himself is presumed unfair under the applicable fiduciary principles, placing the burden on the agent to demonstrate that it was fair. Because Prine's authority rested on a power of attorney executed when Casey lacked the required mental capacity, the subsequent deed was voidable. The court found that Fisher had filed the action within the applicable four-year limitation period. On November 19, 2026, the Eleventh Court of Appeals affirmed the probate court's judgment, leaving Fisher with full ownership of the Milby Road property under her mother's will.You use AI every day. articles.summary: A West Sussex couple won £1 million on the EuroMillions UK Millionaire Maker draw. The win came after months of worry over their baby son’s health.
articles.body: A West Sussex couple won £1 million on the EuroMillions UK Millionaire Maker draw. The win came after months of worry over their baby son’s health. Matt Cole and his fiancée Courtney Cockerton discovered the win after their son Rupert underwent a five-hour operation to repair a cleft lip and palate when he was just 12 weeks old. The family had known before his birth that he would need surgery, but his parents said they were unprepared for the experience.According to the Sussex World, the couple plan to take Rupert and their two-and-a-half-year-old daughter, Ivy, to Disneyland Paris. They also hope to use the winnings to buy a new home and car and provide greater security for their young family.How months of concern over couple’s baby’s health ended with a £1 million winMatt and Courtney had known before Rupert was born that he would need an operation to repair his cleft lip and palate. The procedure took place when he was 12 weeks old and lasted five hours. He also had to stay in hospital overnight. Matt said that knowing about the surgery in advance had not prepared them for seeing their baby go through it at such a young age. The family had faced difficult months around Rupert’s treatment.Matt said, “We’ve been incredibly fortunate that Rupert fed so well when he was born, as cleft conditions can often make feeding difficult. The support we’ve received from NHS staff has been amazing and we’re so grateful for everything they’ve done for us.”The £1 million win turned the couple’s Disneyland Paris dream into a family planThe £1 million win had allowed the couple to plan a trip they had long wanted to take with their children. Matt and Courtney hoped to travel to Disneyland Paris with five-month-old Rupert and their two-and-a-half-year-old daughter, Ivy. They planned to take the Eurostar from St Pancras International Station to Paris Gare du Nord.The journey would be different from their recent trips to London, which had been for Rupert’s medical appointments at Evelina London Children’s Hospital. Courtney said, “We’ve always dreamt of taking her to Disneyland Paris and seeing her face light up when she meets her favourite characters. Now, thanks to this incredible win, that’s the first thing on our list.”How the lottery win brought relief after months of family health worriesCourtney said Rupert’s medical experience had affected the whole family. She also praised Ivy for the way she had responded as the big sister while her younger brother went through treatment.Although Ivy was only two-and-a-half, Courtney said she had been brilliant and had taken everything in her stride. She described her daughter as caring towards Rupert.The couple’s planned visit to Disneyland Paris was intended to create special memories together after the difficult months. Matt said, “Our family and friends have been just as shocked as we are about the win, but they’re absolutely over the moon for us. After everything we’ve been through recently, it feels like we’ve had a really lucky break.”The couple planned to buy a new home and car with their lottery winningsAlongside the Disneyland Paris holiday, Matt and Courtney planned to use their winnings to buy a new home and a new car. The win was expected to give their young family greater security.Matt said, “Through everything that has been happening, I still managed to find time to buy a EuroMillions Lucky Dip ticket. I’m so glad I did – I could never have imagined what would happen next.”“When I realised I’d won £1 million, I genuinely couldn’t believe it. I checked it over and over again. Even now it still hasn’t properly sunk in.”Every EuroMillions entry receives a unique UK Millionaire Maker code, made up of four letters and five numbers. The code is automatically entered into the UK Millionaire Maker draw, held on the same days as the EuroMillions draw.Disclaimer: This article is based on information reported by the Sussex World about Matt Cole and Courtney Cockerton’s £1 million EuroMillions win and their son Rupert’s medical treatment. articles.title: An Italian blacksmith spent more than 50 years building a forest amusement park with 37 handmade rides that run without electricity and are free for visitors
articles.summary: For more than 50 years, Bruno Ferrin from Italy has been turning a patch of woodland near Treviso into an unusual amusement park filled with handmade
articles.body: For more than 50 years, Bruno Ferrin from Italy has been turning a patch of woodland near Treviso into an unusual amusement park filled with handmade rides powered by people and physics rather than conventional electric motors. What began in 1968 as an attempt to run a small food stand on Montello hill gradually grew into Ai Pioppi, a free amusement park containing 37 attractions. Ferrin built the rides himself, often using old steel tubes and discarded materials, despite having no formal training in engineering or physics. The result is an eccentric playground where bicycles, ropes, weights and mechanical forces provide the power.How Bruno Ferrin built ‘Osteria Ai Pioppi’ amusement park despite having no formal training in engineering or physicsFerrin first arrived at the poplar forest on Montello hill near Treviso in 1968, looking for a way to earn money during his spare time. He and his wife, Marisa, established a food and wine stand called Osteria Ai Pioppi, or Tavern at the Poplars, beside a country road near the Piave River.According to Atlas Obscura, the first ride appeared almost by accident. Ferrin wanted to install a swing to attract families but needed two hooks. A local blacksmith told him he could use a welding machine and make them himself. After spending three hours learning to weld, Ferrin returned with the hooks and discovered that he enjoyed creating things from metal.A slide followed, then rocking horses and more attractions. Ferrin soon realised that visitors were coming to the property as much for the rides as for the food. Instead of following a formal business plan, he kept designing and building new attractions one after another. More than 50 years later, the amusement park covers roughly 65,000 square feet of woodland.As per Aipioppi’s official site, Ferrin says, “My life has been intense. With age, strength wanes, but enthusiasm remains that of the first day. For a few years I have been working with my nephew Francesco. We design, build, maintain.”Ferrin, who was born in Treviso in 1937, left compulsory schooling at the age of 10 and worked in several jobs before becoming involved with the restaurant. Although he never had any formal training, he based his craft purely on observation and intuition, which he says he progressively honed.Ai Pioppi's handmade rides use human power and mechanical physicsUnlike conventional amusement parks, Ai Pioppi does not rely on electric motors to operate its attractions. All 37 rides use human effort and mechanical principles to create movement.One of the most striking examples is a 12-foot-high cylindrical centrifuge made from colourful steel tubes. Four people sit at pedalling stations and generate the force needed to rotate the structure. As it spins faster, riders can be pushed against the inside wall by centrifugal force.Ferrin's designs often draw on things he encountered in everyday life. One attraction uses a rope and a weight to lift riders towards the forest canopy, inspired by his childhood experiences helping to swing the enormous bells of a local church. Another ride was inspired by the centrifuge forces he learned about from a television report on Cape Canaveral and astronaut training.The park includes attractions ranging from a 56-foot slide to a 55-ton pendulum. Ferrin works on the rides in his workshop, welding, drilling and painting components. Some projects take weeks, while others can take months or longer depending on what else needs his attention.Why Ferrin's electricity-free amusement park remains free to visitorsFerrin has continued to operate Ai Pioppi according to a philosophy that separates it from conventional commercial amusement parks. The rides are free, with income from the adjoining Osteria Ai Pioppi helping to keep the attraction open without an admission charge.Ferrin has reportedly rejected suggestions from friends that he should introduce even a small entrance fee. His approach is to let visitors eat at the restaurant, enjoy the surrounding forest and then use the rides without paying separately for them.The restaurant itself has become a substantial operation. It can accommodate up to 1,500 diners, while the park and restaurant operate on a seasonal schedule. The site is generally closed during the winter, reopens around late March on weekends and operates daily during August.The park's popularity has grown far beyond the local area. Visitors from Germany and Austria have travelled to Ai Pioppi, while a documentary broadcast on German television helped attract more German-speaking visitors. After the pandemic shutdown, Ferrin's family was reportedly overwhelmed by messages from customers asking when the restaurant and park would reopen.The forest itself is part of Ferrin's unusual amusement park designAi Pioppi is not simply a collection of rides placed inside a forest. Ferrin deliberately works around the existing landscape, sometimes allowing vegetation to grow around the attractions. Wisteria, for example, has enveloped part of a slide's supporting structure.Ferrin told Atlas Obscura that he tries to avoid interfering with plants when positioning a new ride. If a root is in the way, he considers the problem before deciding whether it should be cut. The surrounding landscape also has a significant history: the area near the Piave was part of the frontline between Italian and Austro-Hungarian forces during the First World War, and Ferrin has occasionally encountered remnants of the conflict while digging.Safety is handled separately from Ferrin's informal approach to construction. Although he has no formal physics or engineering qualifications, each attraction is checked by a government-approved engineer, according to the Atlas Obscura report.Bruno Ferrin still builds new rides after more than five decadesFerrin has continued spending several hours a day in his workshop, developing new ideas and maintaining the existing attractions. His approach remains deliberately low-tech, with old steel tubes and other reused materials becoming components of new rides.He has also passed some of his knowledge to his grandson Francesco, who has been involved with the park for decades. Francesco now helps with its digital presence while learning the craft from his grandfather.Ferrin, who was 85, in 2022 when Atlas Obscura visited Ai Pioppi, had no plans to stop building rides. The amusement park that began with a food stand and a pair of handmade swing hooks had become a sprawling collection of mechanical attractions hidden among the trees near Treviso.You use AI every day. articles.title: Bay Area homeowners replacing broken gas furnaces from 2029 may face about $12,500 in additional costs under new emissions rules, with a new analysis finding electric heat-pump installations substantially more expensive
articles.summary: Homeowners across California’s Bay Area could face a significantly higher bill when replacing their natural gas heating systems under an upcoming
articles.body: Homeowners across California’s Bay Area could face a significantly higher bill when replacing their natural gas heating systems under an upcoming emissions regulation. A new assessment by the Bay Area Air Quality Management District, reported by the San Francisco Chronicle and detailed in the district’s November 2026 implementation report, estimates that switching from a conventional gas furnace to an electric heat-pump system could add approximately $12,526 to installation costs for a typical single-family home. The requirement is part of Regulation 9, Rule 4, which aims to eliminate nitrogen oxide (NOx) emissions from newly installed natural gas-fired furnaces. The pollutant contributes to ground-level ozone and particulate pollution, both of which can affect public health and regional air quality. Under the current timeline, the zero-emissions standard will apply to covered furnaces from January 1, 2029. The regulation does not require homeowners to remove existing operational gas furnaces. Instead, it restricts the sale and installation of newly manufactured gas-fired equipment that does not meet the emissions standard, meaning households replacing their systems after the deadline will need to consider compliant alternatives.Heat pumps could significantly increase upfront expensesThe district’s cost assessment highlights the financial difference between conventional heating systems and electric alternatives. Installing a standard natural gas furnace in a single-family home is estimated to cost approximately $8,064, compared with around $20,590 for an electric heat-pump heating and cooling system.This creates an estimated upfront difference of $12,526. However, the financial comparison changes when homeowners also factor in air-conditioning expenses. Since heat pumps provide both heating and cooling, households that would otherwise purchase a separate central air-conditioning system could see the additional cost fall to approximately $2,095. The distinction is particularly relevant in the Bay Area, where an estimated 60% of homes already have central air conditioning. Existing electrical infrastructure and available space for outdoor equipment could also make certain installations less expensive.Electrical upgrades remain a concernWhile heat pumps are expected to offer long-term savings on energy bills, the initial installation could become more complicated for properties requiring electrical upgrades. According to the Air District’s assessment, electrical panel and service upgrades can cost several thousand dollars and, in particularly difficult cases, exceed $20,000. Around 3% of single-family homes and 10% of multifamily properties in California are estimated to have electrical panels that may require upgrades for full electrification.Infrastructure limitations could also affect installation timelines. Data cited in the report indicate that utility service upgrades can take more than 300 days for single-family homes and over 500 days for multifamily buildings. The transition could create additional challenges for apartment owners and tenants, particularly in older buildings where electrical capacity is limited. The district has also identified the possibility of landlords passing some improvement expenses on to renters.Homeowners could save on energy billsDespite the higher upfront investment, electric heat pumps could reduce household energy expenses over time. A study covering three Bay Area climate zones found that households installing minimum-efficiency heat pumps could save between $167 and $474 in their first year. More efficient variable-capacity systems could generate annual savings of approximately $364 to $733, depending on the property and existing equipment.However, the actual savings will vary according to electricity rates, household energy consumption and whether a property already has air conditioning. The availability of financial assistance is another consideration. The Air District’s November assessment noted that federal incentives for residential heat pumps have declined, while state rebates through the TECH Clean California programme were fully subscribed as of September 2026. Several local programmes continue to offer incentives generally ranging from $1,000 to $3,000.Changes to the regulation are still possibleThe 2029 deadline is not entirely settled. The Bay Area Air District has been examining implementation challenges through a working group involving more than 40 stakeholders, including housing representatives, technical experts, manufacturers and government agencies. District staff are scheduled to present their findings to the Board of Directors on December 2, 2026. articles.title: The world has never seen anything like Trump’s surrender in Shenzhen
articles.summary: Congressional Republicans and Democrats should be united in opposing this abomination of U.S. foreign policy.
articles.body:
President Trump regularly boasts that his actions have achieved unique successes that “no one has ever seen before” or “ever thought possible.” But on his brief visit to China last week , he seemed to be trying to replicate an event that was already historic: the 1945 Yalta Conference.

At Yalta, the U.S., Great Britain and the Soviet Union set out to bring an end to World War II, then to arrange for the post-war international order — or, as some would say, to “carve up” the globe into zones of territorial and political dominance for the victors. But now, 82 years later, where Trump goes astray in the implied analogy is that at least the objective of the original meeting was the total defeat of aggression, not its accommodation. Which is to say, Nazi Germany, Fascist Italy and Imperial Japan were certainly not invited to discuss an outcome acceptable to them.

Unlike the Yalta participants — two democracies and one communist dictatorship — the Shenzhen meeting included the dictators of two expansionist powers: communist China’s Xi Jinping, with his aggressive intentions against Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines, and Russia’s Vladimir Putin of formerly communist Russia, the aggressor and accused war criminal in Ukraine who is openly trying to reconstitute the Soviet Empire. They were joined by Trump, who seemed strangely enamored of and obeisant toward the other two.

The prospects of Trump’s meeting do not look any more promising than those of the original Yalta Conference. Franklin Rooevelt, Winston Churchill and Josef Stalin had signed on to the universal principles of non-aggression and secure borders, but Stalin violated his commitments virtually before the ink was dry. Similarly, Xi and Putin have preemptively made clear that under their “no limits strategic partnership,” they will continue to pursue their separate and joint intentions against the U.S.-led world order and against their neighbors.

Those freedom-loving neighbors could count on the U.S. under previous presidents, before the political call to “make America great again” came to mean something quite different for nations reliant on U.S. leadership. In his post-meeting remarks, Trump further downgraded his already diluted commitment to Ukraine’s security , under which he would sell U.S. weapons to NATO allies who could then make them available to Ukraine.

In an absolute boon to Putin and to Xi — who has in no way curtailed his support for Putin’s war — Trump played another pro-Russia card, urging Europeans to end their weapons supply to Ukraine altogether. To ensure that result, the U.S. may stop providing arms to Europeans in the first place.

By these measures, Trump will have completed his tragic transformation of America from supporter of democracies and defender of the victims of aggression to willing participant in the aggression. As Trump might say, no one has ever seen anything like this — certainly not in the 250 years of America’s existence. Congressional Republicans and Democrats should be united in opposing this abomination of U.S. foreign policy.

Joseph Bosco served as China country director for the secretary of Defense from 2005 to 2006 and as Asia-Pacific director of humanitarian assistance and disaster relief from 2009 to 2010. He is a nonresident fellow at the Institute for Corean-American Studies, a member of the advisory board of the Global Taiwan Institute and member of the advisory board of the Vandenberg Coalition.

articles.title: How Brazil’s mosquitoes are helping to fight dengue
articles.summary: Scientists are increasingly using novel ways to re-engineer mosquitoes and use them to battle the diseases they spread.
articles.body:
Scientists in Brazil have successfully tested a novel way of battling dengue – by infecting mosquitoes with harmless bacteria instead of killing them or avoiding their sting.

Researchers presented encouraging results on Saturday at an international conference from a major study that tested thousands of children in Brazil, one of the world’s dengue hotspots.

The testing was done after the research team released millions of mosquitoes that had been re-engineered to carry a naturally occurring bacterium called Wolbachia, which makes it harder for viruses like dengue to grow inside them. The tests indicated dengue infections fell by 68.5 percent.

This is the latest effort to re-engineer mosquitoes to fight the diseases they spread to humans. The research findings were released as the US state of Florida grapples with an outbreak of dengue, thought to be one of the biggest in the United States since the 1940s.

“This is really exciting,” David Hamer, a global health expert at Boston University who wasn’t involved in the Brazilian study, told The Associated Press news agency.

Hamer predicted that using more Wolbachia mosquitoes could “knock dengue down to much lower levels” in many places.

An international team of investigators from Brazil’s Ministry of Health, Emory and Yale universities in the US, and the US National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases conducted the study in Belo Horizonte in southeastern Brazil from 2020 to 2024.

The scientists infected Aedes aegypti mosquitoes with Wolbachia, a naturally occurring bacterium that does not harm humans but can significantly reduce mosquitoes’ ability to transmit some viruses. While the bacterium is present in about 50 percent of insects, the Aedes aegypti – responsible for transmitting dengue, chikungunya, Zika and yellow fever – does not carry it.

Researchers then released the mosquitoes and subsequently tested 5,700 children at random for dengue symptoms, including those living in areas where the infected mosquitoes had been released and those where standard measures like insecticides were used. Researchers also tested for a range of other diseases transmitted by mosquitoes, ticks and sandflies to catch asymptomatic patients.

Only 4 percent of the routine blood tests came back positive in areas where the Wolbachia-engineered mosquitoes were released, compared with 14 percent in other neighbourhoods. Dengue cases fell by 68.5 percent while chikungunya cases were reduced by 73.3 percent, the study found.

The number of dengue infections in Brazil is among the highest in the world, representing about one-tenth of all cases globally. Belo Horizonte, a densely populated city, was in the grips of its worst outbreak during the research period, further showing the efficacy of the Wolbachia method.

The results were presented at a meeting of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene in the US state of Maryland.

No. The World Mosquito Program (WMP) pioneered the Wolbachia method for its ongoing Wolbachia Mosquito Release Project.

The intervention, which has been carried out since the mid-2000s, has focused on regions that include Colombia’s Aburra Valley and the Brazilian city of Niteroi, which have a combined population of about 4.5 million people. Dengue infections there declined by 92 percent in the approximately 1 million people studied, the organisation reported. Researchers emphasised that the method is highly self-sustaining and more environmentally friendly than fumigation, which can be expensive and toxic.

In Singapore, authorities have pursued a Wolbachia-related population suppression approach since 2016. This entails releasing male mosquitoes carrying the bacterium to mate with wild urban females, which then produce eggs that do not hatch.

The scientists’ main aim is to create local populations of Wolbachia-carrying mosquitoes in the study areas. In the WMP intervention, scientists worked with local community leaders to release adult mosquitoes or place their eggs in food takeaway boxes, hoping they would transform into adults and mix with the local mosquito population. Over time, researchers believe, the Wolbachia population will reproduce and become established.

Where else have mosquitoes been used to fight disease?

Mosquitoes, specifically the female Anopheles, also transmit malaria, which is endemic in African countries. Children and pregnant women are most vulnerable to the disease, which can be deadly.

In 2024, researchers from Leiden University Medical Center and Radboud University in the Netherlands engineered mosquitoes to deliver vaccines that could provide immunity against malaria.

They did that by infecting mosquitoes with a modified strain of the malaria parasite, Plasmodium falciparum, which causes the deadliest strain in humans.

The parasite infects humans through mosquito bites. The insect uses its long, needle-like mouth to pierce the skin and inject its saliva into a person’s bloodstream before sucking blood out. Parasites in the saliva, which keeps blood from clotting and dulls pain, then travel directly to the liver, where they rapidly reproduce and infect red blood cells with malaria.

In the trials, researchers mirrored malaria transmission to strengthen liver immunity. However, while 80 percent of one group of participants developed immunity, the trial size was deemed too small to be generalised at just 20 people. It was not clear if the method would be more sustainable than actual vaccines in the long term, the scientists involved said.

Similarly, researchers in the US used the same method in a small trial of 26 participants in 2022 and found that it was 50 percent effective.

Meanwhile, in Japan in 2010, scientists modified mosquitoes to carry a vaccine against leishmaniasis, a parasitic disease typically spread by sandflies. Rodents bitten by the “flying vaccinators” developed antibodies against the parasite.

articles.title: Tories accuse Burnham of turning No 10 into 'joke' after influencer video row
articles.summary: Social media influencer Max Balegde has deleted a video filmed outside the door of Number 10, which was posted on TikTok, in which he mimed along to explicit lyrics.
articles.body:
Andy Burnham has been accused of turning the UK into "a joke" on the world stage by Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, amid a row about social media videos posted from an event in Downing Street.

Social media influencer Max Balegde has deleted a video filmed outside the door of Number 10, which was posted on TikTok, in which he mimed along to explicit lyrics.

Badenoch said it was a "disgrace" that the prime minister allowed 10 Downing Street to be "degraded".

The prime minister's spokesperson said the content was clearly not acceptable and it was "right" that Balegde had taken down the social media posts.

Balegde's video appears to have been filmed earlier this month at an event for around 60 social media influencers hosted by Burnham, who is eager to use social media to reach younger voters. Balegde also gave a speech to those present at the event.

In the video, the influencer, whose real name is Max Trobe, mouths the words "bomboclaat pussywagon chicken nuggets", using audio from a meme that is trending online.

Bomboclaat is a Jamaican profanity referring to a menstrual cloth, while pussy is a slang term for female genitals.

It is unclear when Balegde's video was deleted but it no longer appears on his TikTok or Instagram accounts.

The creator has 3.6 million followers on TikTok and 640,000 on Instagram.

Videos which were filmed inside the Downing Street premises were recorded on government phones, the BBC can reveal.

Attendees at the event have confirmed they had to hand personal devices in and were given a phone and a camera to film with, with the footage they recorded sent to them after the event.

One of the distinctive features of Burnham's time in office has been his enthusiasm for engaging with social media influencers as a means to communicate with different groups of voters, especially younger voters.

It was an approach begun by Sir Keir Starmer, under whom a "new media unit" was formed, but has significantly intensified since July.

The engagement with influencers has elicited criticism of Burnham from those who fear it means reduced scrutiny and diminished opportunities to hold the prime minister to account.

Andy Burnham's plan to collaborate with social media creators

More than £2m spent by government on influencers since July 2024

Speaking at a press conference on Tuesday, Badenoch said she had been "pretty shocked" by the videos coming out of the event, questioning whether they were in good taste.

She said that while Burnham might think he was connecting with young people, many people around the world "will think our country is a joke".

She said: "I do think Andy Burnham should apologise for the way he is using Number 10 as his personal studio to carry out these silly TikToks.

"Vladimir Putin, President Xi and all sorts of other people who are hostile to the UK will see these things, they will get reports of them, and they will see that our prime minister is not a serious man and they will think we are not a serious country."

In a reference to Balegde's video, she said: "I think it is a disgrace that Number 10 – that door which is a symbol of British democracy, power and authority in the world, dignity, that's where we receive people like President Zelensky, showing them that they have the support of people in this country, is being degraded in this way."

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage also criticised the use of the Downing Street door as "puerile" and "demeaning" but said he wouldn't ban influencers from Number 10.

"I wouldn't let them behave quite the way that it happened," he said.

"It showed a slight lack of respect for the place and for the office and was really very inappropriate indeed."

Responding to questions about Balegde's video, the prime minister's spokesperson said "the content was clearly not acceptable", but added "content creators are responsible for what they choose to post".

Asked repeatedly whether Number 10 had requested for the video be removed, the spokesperson said: "It is right the creator took down that content.

"It's clearly not acceptable and that is reflected by the fact that it has been taken down."

They also defended the decision to invite influencers to Downing Street, saying it was "right that the PM listens to" social media content creators who "reach millions of people who don't get their news from traditional media".

Balegde also gave a speech inside the influencers' event, which was held by Burnham in an attempt to build links with a growing sector of the economy.

A smaller group of creators were asked to arrive early to film videos with the prime minister.

One attendee in this group said they had to run ideas past the prime minister's team for approval.

A government spokesperson said they would not comment on security and whether the footage captured on the government phones was reviewed, but said it was "not abnormal" for attendees of Downing Street to use government phones.

articles.title: Syria land mine casualties soar, two years after war
articles.summary: Nearly 1,000 children are among those killed or injured by explosives left over from the conflict, figures show.
articles.body:
Eleven-year-old Alaa was tending her family's goats with her siblings in a field behind their home in Umm Khuzaym, north-west Syria, on Sunday when there was a flash and a deafening bang.

"Then we heard people screaming," Alaa's father, Walid Mohammed Al-Ghafar, told the BBC.

Walid ran outside to find his daughter lying face down, killed, and her 10-year-old brother, Mahmoud, seriously injured.

Unwittingly, the children had triggered a landmine.

The incident and others this week bring to nearly 1,000 the number of children killed or injured by explosive ordnance in Syria since the fall of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, according to the UN Mine Action Service (Unmas).

The village is one of many where families have returned to homes and farmland that were once on the front lines of Syria's 13-year civil war.

Alaa's father said demining teams had visited several times to clear the fields. He and other residents believed it was safe for farmers and children to move around.

But mines and other explosives can lie far beyond former battle lines, making it difficult to establish which areas are safe.

"Remnants of war from today's conflicts are often very widely and broadly scattered, often without patterns, which makes it extremely difficult to do clearance," Katrin Atkins, research lead at Landmine Monitor, a global mine monitoring initiative, told the BBC.

The dangers are reflected in a sharp rise in casualties across Syria.

A total of 1,602 people were killed or injured by landmines and explosive remnants of war in 2025 alone, an increase of more than 50% on the previous year, according to the Landmine Monitor report, published by the International Campaign to Ban Landmines on Tuesday.

Only Myanmar, with 1,891 casualties, recorded more.

The report attributes the rise in Syria partly to the large-scale return of refugees and internally displaced people following Assad's overthrow.

"When you look at population movement, a couple of months later you see an increase of incidents in these areas, because that's exactly where people go and start to use the fields again," Atkins said.

More than 60% of casualties recorded by the world's largest landmine clearance charity, the Halo Trust, involve farming, agriculture or shepherding, according to its Syria programme manager, Simon Jackson.

"They're not going to wait for the government or for organisations like us to come and tell them that everything is safe and clear," he told the BBC. "People are taking risks out of desperation."

Since Assad's fall on 8 December 2024, Unmas has recorded at least 1,556 incidents in Syria involving explosive ordnance.

They have caused 2,701 casualties: 935 people killed and 1,766 injured. Children account for 995 of those victims, or about 37%.

But the toll is likely to be higher, with experts estimating that overall casualties could be under-reported by 25-50%.

For many of those who survive, the consequences are devastating and permanent.

Majid Abdul Rahman, 27, was travelling in a car in the Ghouta region on the outskirts of Damascus in March 2025 when it struck an explosive device. The vehicle filled with smoke and he felt a pain in his leg.

More than a year later, Majid has difficulty walking and has been unable to return to work, leaving him struggling to provide for his family.

The danger has continued into this month, with at least 20 people killed and more than 40 injured by explosive ordnance in November.

In one of the worst recorded incidents, an explosion in a school courtyard in Hasakah on 4 November killed a 12-year-old and injured 19 others. And on Monday, a 13-year-old boy was killed when an unexploded cluster munition detonated in southern Daraa province.

The threat is also holding back Syria's economic recovery. Contaminated farmland cannot be safely cultivated, while people collecting scrap metal or trying to salvage materials from abandoned areas also risk triggering explosions.

The Syrian Ministry of Defence says since the end of 2024 its teams have found and dealt with more than 315,000 mines and unexploded munitions.

But no nationwide survey has established how much land remains contaminated, making it difficult to assess the full scale of the problem.

"We're in a bit of a black hole," Atkins said.

And with the extent of contamination still largely unknown, the war continues to claim victims two years after it ended.

articles.title: UK police arrest two after break-in at Prince William’s country residence

Two men have been arrested on suspicion of ⁠⁠⁠⁠burglary and ⁠⁠⁠⁠trespass after a break-in at the country residence of Britain’s Prince William and Princess Catherine in eastern England, according to police.

The suspects were arrested on Tuesday after officers were called on Monday night in response to a report of suspicious activity at a property on ⁠⁠⁠⁠the royal family’s Sandringham estate in Norfolk. The property was unoccupied at the time, police added.

The Sun newspaper first reported that police were investigating a break-in at Anmer Hall, a 10-bedroom house, which the late Queen Elizabeth gave William and Catherine as a wedding present in 2011.

The men were arrested after a search involving police dogs, drones and a helicopter.

Although William and Catherine use the country retreat for holidays and short breaks, their main home is on the Windsor Castle estate, west of London.

The news ⁠⁠⁠⁠came as William visited Prime Minister Andy ⁠⁠⁠⁠Burnham at the British leader’s office in the capital.

Intruders have breached royal properties several times over the years.

In October 2024, burglars broke into the Windsor Castle estate west of London and stole a pick-up truck and a quad bike from a farm building.

King Charles III and Queen Camilla were not in the castle at the time, but it was reported that William and Catherine were in their nearby house.

Three years earlier, a man armed with a crossbow was detained on the castle grounds. Jaswant Singh Chail was later sentenced to nine years in prison after admitting he had been encouraged by a chatbot to kill Queen Elizabeth.

In 1982, intruder Michael Fagan managed to sneak into the monarch’s private chambers while she was in bed. The queen spent 10 minutes chatting with the burglar before raising the alarm when he asked for a cigarette.

Fagan was sent to a psychiatric hospital, then released and later jailed for unrelated criminal offences.

articles.title: Record 5,200 heat-linked deaths estimated in England this year
articles.summary: The UK Health Security Agency says this year's number of deaths is twice that of the previous record year.
articles.body:
More than 5,000 people suffered heat-associated deaths in England this summer, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has estimated - the highest number since records began in 2016.

The UK experienced its hottest summer on record in 2026, and the estimated 5,258 heat-linked deaths were twice the previous high of 2,985 in 2022.

The most deadly period of the year for heat-related deaths was between 21 and 28 June, when there were an estimated 2,401 heat-associated deaths. Temperatures peaked at 38C in that period.

Climate change is expected to increase the length, frequency and intensity of extreme heat, the UKHSA has warned.

The UKHSA said summer 2026 was "exceptional", and that it recorded the highest annual number of heat episodes, which it defines as days when the average Central England Temperature (CET) is at least 20C.

There were seven heat episodes between May and August, adding up to a total of 41 days.

The UK experienced widespread heatwaves as 2026 became the hottest summer on record, according to provisional data from the Met Office.

A heatwave in May smashed the temperature record for that month by more than 2C, with a high of 35.1C recorded at Kew Gardens.

A month later, June's heatwave set another monthly temperature record - 38.0C in Lingwood, Norfolk. The previous high was 35.6C set in 1957 and equalled during the infamous 1976 heatwave.

Both were caused by heat domes - stalled areas of high pressure that trap hot air over the region.

Another heatwave in mid-August saw temperatures climb as high as 38.2C at Hartpury College in Gloucestershire, making it the hottest day of the year.

The UK's hottest day on record was 19 July 2022, when temperatures hit 40.3C in Coningsby, Lincolnshire.

A lack of rainfall this year also saw droughts declared in all of Wales and more than two-thirds of England, while wildfires caused devastation in some parts of the country.

UKHSA said the findings "underline the need for longer-term adaptation" to a warming climate, and that adapting homes, neighbourhoods and health and care settings would be "increasingly important".

Dr Ross Thompson, principal environmental health scientist at UKHSA, said this summer's hot weather had a substantial impact on public health, "particularly during the early heat episodes in May and June".

He added that periods of extreme heat are expected to become "longer, more frequent and more intense" as the climate continues to warm.

Speaking in the Commons, Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said she wanted "to offer the deepest condolences to all those who lost a loved one this summer".

"The numbers are a stark reminder of the human impact of climate change, and that is why I have asked the NHS to now prepare for summer as seriously as we do for winter," she said.

During a speech at the COP31 summit earlier this month, Prime Minister Andy Burnham spoke about the extreme weather experienced in the UK this summer, describing it as "not normal".

In a public message, the SP chief asked Congress to hold "serious discussions" on the seat-sharing deal.In a lengthy social media post on X, Akhilesh said the INDIA bloc had a "historic opportunity" to defeat the "communal BJP and its narrow-minded allies" once and for all."This time, we have a historic opportunity to come together as the two secular parties and defeat the communal BJP and its narrow-minded allies once and for all, saving the country from falling into the wrong hands and being ruined," the SP chief said."We want you and us to hold serious discussions, taking public expectations and realities into account, to ensure our ‘alliance’ wins in most constituencies. Among the seats you and we contest, the number we win should exceed the number we lose. Only victory will make the division of seats respectable, because only the seats we win will bring us respect," he added.He also urged Congress to identify and send potential seats in addition to the 26 seats discussed during the seat-sharing meeting."Therefore, in addition to the 26 seats from the priority list your team provided that we have discussed today, please identify and send us all other potential seats. Then we will sit down together and assess which seats, and which candidates for those seats, are in a winning position. Based on our assessment and the mathematical equation for victory, we may also be able to tell the Congress about many winnable seats it has not even considered for some reason," Akhilesh said."Our aim is that when the senior leaders meet, the discussion should be about candidates for the ‘INDIA alliance’ in every constituency, not Congress or SP candidates. And the best and most positive outcome would be for us to present our candidates as ‘PDA candidates’," he added.Simultaneosly, Samajwadi Party also released its first list of candidates for the assembly elections, naming five nominees from constituencies including Saharanpur, Shamli, Amroha, and Lalitpur.Also Read: Samajwadi Party releases first list of 5 candidates as seat-sharing talks with Congress continueReportedly, Congress was seeking two seats in Saharanpur region.This comes after Akhilesh said that the SP had offered 26 seats to Congress as the parties held the first round of seat-sharing talks.The statement comes amid ongoing political discussions over seat-sharing and coordination ahead of the 2027 assembly elections in the state.Earlier in the day, SP chief Akhilesh Yadav said senior leaders entrusted with the negotiations were actively engaged in discussions, but a final decision had not yet been reached.Meanwhile, leaders from both Congress and the Samajwadi Party indicated that negotiations were moving in a positive direction.The SP is seeking a major political comeback in 2027 after consecutive defeats in the 2017 and 2022 assembly elections.In the 2022 assembly elections, which the two parties contested separately, the SP won 111 of the 347 seats it contested, while Congress secured two of the 399 seats on which it fielded candidates.In the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, which both parties contested under the INDIA bloc banner, the Samajwadi Party secured 37 of the 62 seats it contested, while Congress won six of the 17 seats it contested.Uttar Pradesh, which has 403 Assembly seats, is expected to witness a major contest between the BJP and the SP in 2027, while Congress is also seeking to expand its political footprint in the state.Get the latest India News and Live updates.
