articles.title: US sanctions on Lebanon’s Hezbollah-affiliates may have limited impact
articles.summary: Analysts say US sanctions unlikely to weaken Hezbollah significantly, but risk hurting everyday Lebanese.
articles.body:
Beirut, Lebanon – New United States sanctions on an organisation linked to the Iranian-backed Lebanese group Hezbollah will have a limited impact beyond the political messaging the punishment provides, analysts have told Al Jazeera.

The organisation – a charity called Wa Ta’awanu Association – was among the entities and individuals targeted by the US Treasury in new sanctions announced on November 18, accusing it of being a “front organisation” for Hezbollah. The Treasury said the sanctions were an effort to disrupt Hezbollah’s financing networks.

The sanctions are part of a US campaign against Hezbollah, a Shia political and military group. Washington has put pressure on the Lebanese government to make progress on disarming Hezbollah, which has been engaged in an on-off war with Israel for the past 40 years.

But experts told Al Jazeera, the sanctions will do little to change Lebanon’s domestic situation, in which Hezbollah has been one of the major powers – if not the major power – over the past two decades.

“[The US] is threatening to impose sanctions on political, judicial and security figures but that won’t change the reality,” Qassem Kassir, a Lebanese journalist close to Hezbollah, told Al Jazeera. “Sanctions or the threat of sanctions will not change the reality inside Lebanon.”

Lebanese media reports have suggested that the US, frustrated by the Lebanese government’s lack of progress in disarming the Iran-backed group, could apply sanctions beyond direct Hezbollah affiliates and start to target bankers and businessmen.

“There are other packages, a second, third, maybe a fourth [round of sanctions],” Ali Hamade, a Lebanese journalist with Annahar, claimed in a video posted to social media. “It will focus on Hezbollah funding and money smuggling efforts and may involve several bankers, figures in the world of Lebanese finance and business, in the real estate sector and contractors.

He added that politicians, security personnel, judges, and figures in Lebanese public administration were unlikely to face sanctions yet.

Targeting Hezbollah-affiliated organisations

Hezbollah, a Shia-dominated movement which emerged during the Lebanese civil war, is part of a wider network of Iran-linked groups in the region. The group is believed to receive direct financing from Tehran, as well as its own financing networks.

In its sanctions announcement, the US Treasury claimed that the Wa Ta’awanu Association “provides cover for Hizballah’s activities under the guise of delivering humanitarian services”.

But Kassir said the group provided assistance to needy Lebanese people.

“Unfortunately, the Americans and some Lebanese parties want to prevent any assistance or service from reaching people,” he said. “However, sanctions will not stop the work of the Wa Ta’awanu Association, just as it has not been able to stop the Al Qard Al Hassan, educational institutions, construction companies and Jihad Al-Binaa.”

Al Qard Al Hassan , a financial institution, and Jihad Al-Binaa, a construction company, are part of a wide array of Hezbollah-affiliated organisations that have been sanctioned by the US, though both companies also employ or serve people not affiliated with Hezbollah.

Israel has continued to attack what it says are Hezbollah targets in Lebanon intermittently, despite a “ceasefire” agreement earlier this year.

It also continues to hold territory it invaded up to 10km (6.2 miles) into Lebanese territory.

Israel – backed by the US – has tied its withdrawal from Lebanon to the full disarmament of Hezbollah. Talks between the Israeli and Lebanese governments were held earlier this year and led to a Framework Agreement in June, which designated so-called “pilot zones” where Israeli troops would withdraw, and the Lebanese army would deploy to disarm Hezbollah.

But the pilot zone programme has had little success, as Israel still refuses to withdraw from new territories and accuses the Lebanese army of failing to disarm Hezbollah in the existing pilot zones.

In the meantime, the US has looked for other means to pressure Hezbollah, as it continues attacks against the group’s patron, Iran.

“The US treats sanctions as one of several forms of pressure that it can exert on Hezbollah’s financial networks,” David Wood, the senior Lebanon analyst with International Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera. “Washington has also targeted Hezbollah’s efforts to raise money outside of traditional financial systems – such as receiving physical cash – by insisting that the Lebanese state exert more control over the country’s airport, seaports and border with neighbouring Syria.”

But Wood argued that sanctions against the group and individuals connected to it are only likely to have a limited effect.

“The threat of US sanctions might change the behaviour of some Lebanese elites, but that source of leverage largely disappears after imposing sanctions, because it is not straightforward to lift them,” Wood said. “Imposing US sanctions seeks to raise the cost of doing business with Hezbollah, especially for alleged associates of the party who enjoy lucrative sources of private income. This tactic is probably less effective in relation to direct affiliates of Hezbollah, which are more likely to operate outside traditional financial networks already.”

Analysts also argue that the US’s use of sanctions is politically driven, showing that it is not a neutral or balanced actor when it comes to brokering deals between Beirut and Tel Aviv.

“The US is not a fair or equal decision-maker because it is a strategic partner of Israel and that’s the motivation behind sanctions,” Karim Safieddine, a Beirut-based nonresident fellow at the Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy, told Al Jazeera. “Sanctions by, say, the UN or independent bodies or courts that actually assess Hezbollah’s criminal culpability are one thing. But partisan sanctions that are part of warfare obviously only induce further [divisions] in Lebanon and have had lots of repercussions on people who are not Hezbollah.”

The US pressure campaign is still having an adverse effect on Lebanese people who do not support, or in some cases, actively oppose Hezbollah, due to the affiliation of the Shia community with the group – a connection the group itself also stresses at times.

“There are real repercussions on normal Lebanese people, especially Shia, because of supposed affiliations within a party that is very embedded in a community,” Safieddine said. “And it’s very hard to disembed it, as opposed to the genocidal tactics used by Israel. But the issue with sanctions is that they’re not actually based on criteria of human rights respectability.”

articles.title: Cameroon separatist leader pleads not guilty at war crimes trial in Norway
articles.summary: Lucas Cho Ayaba is accused of remotely planning attacks that killed and injured dozens of civilians.
articles.body:
Cameroonian separatist leader Lucas Cho Ayaba has pleaded not guilty in a Norwegian court to being an accessory to war crimes and “terrorism”, charges that carry a sentence of up to 30 years.

The 54-year-old, who appeared in a court in Oslo on Tuesday, is accused of involvement in planning two attacks in Cameroon from Norway, helping to select targets and pay for explosives.

Prosecutors say Ayaba, also known as Cho Lucas Yabah, remotely led the separatist Amazonia Governing Council and commanded its armed wing, the Amazonia Defence Forces, from 2017 until 2024, when he was arrested in Norway, where he has lived since 2008.

Francophone-majority Cameroon has been gripped for nearly 10 years by conflict between state security forces and separatists demanding the independence of two Anglophone regions in the country’s west to form what supporters call “Ambazonia”.

In February 2023, three improvised devices exploded during a mountain run race near Buea in southwestern Cameroon, killing a 38-year-old woman and injuring 19 civilians.

In February of the following year, another improvised device killed a 15-year-old girl during a Youth Day celebration in Nkambe, northwestern Cameroon. More than 90 civilians were wounded, with some undergoing amputations.

Ayaba is also alleged to have encouraged or ordered the murder or attempted murder of captives and to have orchestrated the torture or humiliation of four women accused of having intimate relations with Cameroonian soldiers.

“Messages on WhatsApp are key evidence in this case,” prosecutor Carl Fredrik Fari told the AFP news agency.

“Wrap a rope around his neck and send him to hell,” Ayaba allegedly said in an audio message sent on WhatsApp in October 2023, after receiving videos showing a mistreated prisoner believed to be a Cameroonian soldier.

Ayaba’s lawyer, Morten Engesbak, told AFP that Ayaba “sees himself as the leader of a struggle to liberate a population that has been oppressed for very many years by the Cameroonian authorities”.

The unrest began in late 2016 after Anglophone lawyers and teachers protested against the appointment of Francophone magistrates unfamiliar with British common law to courts in English-speaking regions, and French-speaking teachers unable to communicate fluently in English.

The protests were met with a violent government crackdown and eventually gave rise to a separatist movement seeking independence for the two regions.

The UN says at least 6,000 civilians have been killed since 2016. More than 330,000 people were displaced within Cameroon in 2026 and another 100,000 took refuge in neighbouring Nigeria.

The trial in the Oslo district court is expected to last until March 12.

articles.title: Sacked London Pride boss given suspended prison sentence
articles.summary: The sentencing brings a long-running legal battle to an end.
articles.body:
The sacked boss of London Pride has been handed a suspended prison sentence after "harvesting" confidential documents to disrupt an investigation into his alleged misconduct and set up his own rival company.

London's High Court heard how Christopher Joell-Deshields had downloaded more than 50 private documents just days after agreeing to a court order to hand over all company property.

Mr Justice Cotter said the 55-year-old had downloaded documents on a "large and significant scale" with the intention of "disrupting the organisation" and "advancing his own causes".

Lawyers for Joell-Deshields said he had mental health issues and couldn't recall deliberately downloading private information.

The former Pride in London (PIL) chief executive was held in contempt on two separate counts, after admitting failing to hand back company property and failing to provide a witness statement confirming he had done so.

He was sentenced to six months imprisonment for the first count, and four months for the second.

Both sentences were suspended for 18 months, with Cotter warning the defendant the court would "not be in any way likely to be as lenient if there were to be any further breaches".

The sentencing brings to a close a long-running legal battle between the organisers of the UK's largest pride event and its former boss.

Joell-Deshields was suspended in August 2025 after being accused of bullying and misappropriating vouchers donated by a sponsor in order to purchase luxury perfumes and Apple products. He denies those claims.

Staff at UK's largest Pride event allege bullying and misconduct under sacked CEO

The court heard how within days of his suspension, employees of PIL were frozen out of key operational systems needed to run the organisation, including financial accounts, emails and social media, which led to the organisers seeking an injunction in the High Court.

At a hearing on 12 September last year, Joell-Deshields agreed to a court order to hand back various documents and company property, including plans for holding a Pride event in London's Vauxhall Pleasure Gardens.

Evidence provided to the court by Pride in London showed how, within days of signing the order, Joell-Deshields went on to download more than 50 private documents, including some relating to the internal investigation into his alleged misconduct.

Caley Wright, representing Joell-Deshields, told the court that, despite his earlier admissions, his client did "not recall" that he "set out to deliberately harvest documents".

Handing down the sentence, Cotter told the court that Joell-Deshields had "persistently failed to be fully open and honest about the extent of his breaches" and that his conduct amounted to "wilful, flagrant and deliberate disobedience".

He added: "Anyone who chooses to act in such a fashion, harvesting documentation rather than giving them back, must face the court recognising it as a serious and flagrant breach which requires the court to act to protect its own rules and orders.

"Such behaviour will not be tolerated, and it does not overstate matters to say the rule of law will suffer otherwise."

In April 2026 it was announced Joell-Deshields had been dismissed from his role at Pride in London following an internal investigation and an unsuccessful appeal.

The court heard how his dismissal was subject to separate ongoing employment tribunal proceedings.

articles.title: A West Texas family wanted its ranchland to become part of Big Bend National Park; a US House panel has advanced a bill allowing about 6,100 acres to be added through voluntary donation or exchange
articles.summary: For some families, land is much more than a piece of property that can be bought or sold.
articles.body: For some families, land is much more than a piece of property that can be bought or sold. It carries generations of memories, stories and connections, becoming part of their identity over the years. And sometimes, preserving that connection means allowing the land to become part of something much larger than the family itself.A family ranch, especially, is much bigger than the land itself. Held within it are not only the beloved elders but also the love that was once shared, the words that were exchanged and the lives that were lived to the fullest. And this is what makes a recent development in West Texas particularly meaningful.According to an announcement from the office of US Congressman August Pfluger website, the House Committee on Natural Resources has advanced the Big Bend National Park Boundary Adjustment Act. The proposed legislation would allow approximately 6,100 acres along Terlingua Creek, west of the park, to be added to Big Bend National Park through voluntary donation or exchange.How the Fulcher family’s ranchland could become part of Big Bend National ParkFor the Fulcher family, the idea of seeing their ranchland become part of Big Bend National Park has been a long-standing wish. The family has lived in West Texas for generations and owned land along Terlingua Creek, just west of the national park. Rather than seeing the property remain outside the park's boundaries, they wanted the landscape to become part of a larger conservation effort, where it could be protected for generations to come.However, transferring privately owned land into a national park is not as simple as handing over the property. The Big Bend Conservancy, the park's nonprofit partner, has been working with the Fulcher family and other willing landowners to make the expansion possible. According to the Conservancy's director, the organisation purchased the land from the family rather than receiving it as a direct donation. It now plans to donate the acquired property to the National Park Service once the necessary legislation is approved.The proposed expansion covers approximately 6,100 acres along the park's western boundary, including land around Terlingua Creek. The area also contains existing housing structures that could potentially be used by park staff and law enforcement personnel while patrolling the region. Since only Congress can authorise changes to a national park's boundaries, the Conservancy needs the proposed legislation to move forward before the land can formally become part of Big Bend.The important part of the proposal is that the land can only be acquired through voluntary donation or exchange. It expressly prohibits the use of eminent domain or condemnation, meaning private landowners cannot be forced to give up their property for the expansion.Why the proposed expansion matters for Big Bend National ParkThe decision is about more than just integrating additional land into the park. The proposed expansion could help protect a landscape that holds considerable ecological and historical value. The area along Terlingua Creek is particularly important as it contains a riparian habitat, where the presence of water supports a variety of plants and wildlife in an otherwise arid region. The land also contains fossil beds, heritage homesteads and areas used by nesting birds. Protecting these spaces would help preserve not just the natural landscape but also the history and biodiversity associated with it.The Big Bend Conservancy has been working towards this expansion for several years, acquiring parcels from willing landowners so they can eventually be added to the park. Its conservation efforts are intended to keep these landscapes protected rather than leave them vulnerable to future changes in land use. If the legislation moves forward, the additional acreage would become part of a much larger effort to preserve the natural and historical character of the Big Bend region.In the end, the Fulcher family's wish is about more than adding a few thousand acres to a national park. It is also about what happens to a piece of land after the generations who called it home are gone. Ranches, farms and family properties often carry stories that cannot be measured by their size or market value, and preserving them sometimes means allowing them to become part of something beyond private ownership. articles.title: Emir of Daura: Nigerian monarch suspended over sexual assault claims
articles.summary: The Emir of Daura is one of Nigeria's best-known monarchs, with politicians often trying to gain his support.
articles.body:
One of Nigeria's best-known monarchs, the Emir of Daura, has been suspended from all official engagements and travel following allegations of sexual assault by a Polish tourist.

The visitor said Umar Farouk Umar, 92, had grabbed her chest during a tourism encounter and that she felt disgusted by the experience.

The allegation sparked widespread discussion across social media platforms, with many calling for the suspension of the emir and an investigation - calls the Katsina state government has now heeded.

Umar has not commented on the allegations or his suspension.

He is one of several emirs - a traditional role dating back to pre-colonial times - who still wield great cultural and religious influence in northern Nigeria, although they have lost their political power.

Daura, where Umar serves as emir, holds an extremely important position for the Hausa people who dominate northern Nigeria. It is widely regarded as their spiritual homeland and the origin of the Hausa royal lineage, serving as the core of Hausa origin mythology and the legitimate foundation of traditional authority.

Politicians routinely visit his palace for royal prayers and to gain his support.

On her Instagram page, the tourist said she had spent 30 days travelling around Nigeria before visiting the Emir's palace on 14 November.

She posted a video, which has since been deleted, in which a man who appears to be the emir is holding her hands in his lap.

After some moments she was heard saying: "Stop, stop" as the hands reached for her chest.

According to a statement, Katsina Governor Dikko Umaru Radda directed the immediate constitution of a committee to investigate the allegations.

The statement said the state government was taking the allegations seriously and would rely on the committee's findings to determine the appropriate course of action.

It said the committee's findings and recommendations would be fully implemented, stressing that justice would be served.

However, it did not disclose the membership of the investigative committee, its terms of reference or the timeline for submitting its report.

The emir has been on the throne since 2007, succeeding his brother Bashar dan Umaru, who reigned for 41 years.

articles.title: Substance at Don Toliver Manchester show may be linked to robberies, police say
articles.summary: Police are investigating a possible link between the Co-op Live evacuation and reported robberies.
articles.body:
An "unknown substance" that prompted a mass evacuation at a rap concert may be linked to robberies and stolen jewellery at the venue, police have said.

More than 12,000 people were evacuated from Manchester's Co-op Live during a performance by US rapper Don Toliver on Sunday.

One person was taken to hospital and 88 others were treated at the scene after concertgoers reported a "horrible smell" and some people "coughing up blood".

Greater Manchester Police (GMP) said officers received nine reports of jewellery being stolen during the concert but no arrests had been made and the substance had not yet been identified.

Assistant Chief Constable Tom Harding said there was "no wider ongoing risk" to the public.

"We are aware similar robberies have been reported at two European concerts for the same artist and will be linking in with our European counterparts to better understand the wider picture of this suspected offending," he said.

In a statement on Tuesday evening, Co-op Live said it was conducting a "full review" into the incident.

"The safety and security of our guests, artists and staff remain our highest priority, and we take that responsibility extremely seriously."

The venue, which opened in 2024, apologised to fans for what should have been an "enjoyable evening" and said it expects no disruption to future events.

The substance was released at around 22:00 GMT, near the end of Toliver's show as part of his Nitrous – Octane world tour.

Afterwards, 88 people underwent dry decontamination at the scene and were accommodated at the neighbouring Etihad Stadium while the incident was managed.

Many were advised to seal their clothes in a bag overnight.

Poppy Rutter and Sophie Billing, both 19, who had travelled from Cambridge to see the concert, said it was not immediately clear what had happened.

Sophie said: "I thought something had gone wrong with smoke coming off stage.

"We started to suffer, coughing and spluttering and feeling tight-chested. A member of staff said it was tear gas.

"Security rushed in and went straight to the pit. We only left as we were starting to feel unsafe and not 100 per cent well."

She said there was "no communication", adding: "You would think Manchester would be extra vigilant, given what's happened in the past."

Posting on Instagram on Monday, Toliver said: "I just wanna make sure everyone is safe and the next show goes on properly. My heart and prayers are with everyone that was injured last night at Co-op Live.

"The only thing I love more than creating music is performing for my fans."

He also asked that people stop bringing substances into his shows.

GMP urged anyone who feels unwell or develops symptoms following the concert to seek medical advice.

articles.title: Zelensky seeks reinforcements from Democrats if Trump’s diplomacy falters
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky is seeking reinforcement against his country’s conflict with Russia from Democrats in the new year if President Trump’s diplomacy falters. Zelensky has been vocal about pursuing tougher sanctions against Russia but asked Ukrainian allies to “cover our needs for at least the whole of December” in an interview with Bloomberg on…
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky is seeking reinforcement against his country’s conflict with Russia from Democrats in the new year if President Trump’s diplomacy falters.

Zelensky has been vocal about pursuing tougher sanctions against Russia but asked Ukrainian allies to “cover our needs for at least the whole of December” in an interview with Bloomberg on Monday.

“Why? Because I’m still counting on being able to find, so to speak, a new approach to the new Congress in January or February,” he stated.

His comments are referring to the Democratic Party securing control of the Senate and House in November’s midterm elections. Congressional Democrats criticized Trump for the Russian diesel deal and for recently calling Russian President Vladimir Putin his “friend.”

“America itself is putting itself in a very uncomfortable position,” Zelensky remarked while speaking with the outlet. “Politically, it looks as though it is pursuing the same course as Putin, who wants to force Ukraine to capitulate.”

“There must be such a level of support for Ukraine and such sanctions that they send a clear signal to the Russians … it’s time to sit down at the negotiating table and end the war,” the Ukrainian president continued.

Russian drones struck an apartment building north of Kyiv on Sunday, according to Reuters . The attacks killed at least four people and left up to a dozen more buried in the rubble.

On the same day, Zelensky confirmed Ukrainian drones sank a Russian naval ship in a Libyan port.

Ukrainian leaders criticized Russia for targeting civilian areas as Zelensky renewed his calls for Patriot missile interceptors , which he stated are paramount to shooting down Russian missiles and drones targeting the country’s cities.

“It’s very unpleasant that amid all the bargaining over how to end the war, Ukraine is facing not only cuts in supplies of Patriot interceptors but also delays in deliveries,” Zelensky told Bloomberg.

U.S.-backed talks between Kyiv and Moscow resumed this month with special envoy Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, saying they were making progress .

“A final agreement will require difficult decisions. But we are making progress, in close coordination with Russia, Ukraine, and Europe, toward an outcome that can end this war, strengthen European security, and create the foundations for lasting peace,” Kushner wrote on social media last week.

articles.title: Pope Francis’ private diary reveals visions of the devil
articles.summary: The book, “The Private Diary of Pope Francis,” also shows the pope went through a deep spiritual crisis in 2021 and 2022.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Pope Francis wrote that he saw the devil multiple times and felt he had seen the “gates of Hell” amid the fallout from the handling of the clergy sexual abuse scandal in Chile , according to excerpts from his personal diary the Vatican published Tuesday.

The book, “The Private Diary of Pope Francis,” also shows the pope went through a deep spiritual crisis in 2021 and 2022, in which he described being tempted to abuse his power to act with ultimate authority.

The book was released simultaneously worldwide in five languages and distributed in 94 countries.

Francis, born Jorge Mario Bergoglio, was the leader of the Catholic Church from March 13, 2013 until his death on April 21, 2025.

Pope Francis saw Devil 3 times, describes ‘raspy’ voice

In his entries, selected by his close friend Cardinal Víctor Manuel Fernández for the book, Francis wrote that he “clearly heard the voice of the Devil.” He described seeing him once from a car and another time in the choir loft during Mass while he was in Buenos Aires. He wrote that he could not forget the devil’s “menacing” eyes, according to Vatican News .

The third vision came after Francis’ 2018 trip to Chile, during which he received wide backlash for dismissing claims made by victims of the Rev. Fernando Karadima . He later apologized and admitted he had made serious mistakes.

He wrote a few months after the trip that he “saw the entrance to Hell. Pagan seduction in full force” in the scandal.

In a 2021 entry, Francis wrote that he saw and heard the devil a few days after returning to Rome from the trip.

“‘Now I’ve gotten everything I wanted,'” Francis quoted the devil saying. “Just as I can’t forget his eyes from the previous two, in this case, I can’t forget the powerful raspiness of his voice.”

Pope Francis experienced spiritual crisis, temptation to abuse power

The book shows Francis’ spiritual crisis beginning Jan. 24, 2021. He’d canceled multiple public appearances the day prior, which the Vatican attributed to a flare-up of back and nerve pain. Francis revealed in his entries that he was suffering an intestinal problem that led to the removal of 13 inches of his colon.

For Francis, the temptation he faced during this time to use his power in an authoritarian fashion was the devil pushing him toward “reductive curiosity.” By the end of 2022, he said, he came through the crisis by placing his trust in God.

Francis kept the diary in a leather-bound calendar he used as a notebook. The entries begin in 1992 and follow his time as an assistant bishop in Buenos Aires to his years as the city’s cardinal archbishop and finally his time as pope. The last entry is dated Aug. 18, 2024.

The diary does not include Francis’ full thoughts. Entries were selected and contextualized by Fernández, who says Francis wrote his most private thoughts in code.

articles.title: Twitch streamer Bryce Arky claims OSCS is ‘done’ as fans question group’s future after latest livestream
articles.summary: Twitch streamer Bryce “Arky” has said that content group OSCS (On Some Chill ****) is over and its members will stop making videos together.
articles.body: Twitch streamer Bryce “Arky” has said that content group OSCS (On Some Chill ****) is over and its members will stop making videos together. During a recent Just Chatting stream, the 26-year-old told an associate that the group would no longer create content and that its members would simply remain friends living in the same house. He also suggested that OSCS could officially come to an end in early 2027. However, Arky said the group might continue talking about a possible return before making its final decision clear. His comments have also led to mixed reactions from fans on X.Bryce “Arky” Explains Why OSCS Will Stop Making Videos as Fans Question His Latest ClaimOn November 22, 2026, X user @yoxics shared one-minute clip from Arky's recent livestream. In the video, someone asked the streamer whether OSCS was actually over. Arky answered yes and made it clear that the group would no longer produce videos together.He said, "Yeah. Actually. Yeah. Yeah. OSCS is done. No more videos, we do nothing; we're just like friends that live in a crib."His associate did not seem convinced and asked whether he was being serious or simply joking. Arky repeated that the group was over, leaving little room for doubt about what he was saying during the stream.However, the streamer also explained that an official announcement might not come immediately. articles.title: Turkish military helicopter crash kills five in western Turkiye
articles.summary: The Defence Ministry did not elaborate on the cause of the crash, days after another deadly army helicopter accident.
articles.body:
A Turkish Air Force helicopter has crashed in western Turkiye, killing five crew members, according to the country’s Ministry of National Defence.

The accident occurred on Tuesday, 12 days after similar accident killed four people.

“An AS-532 helicopter belonging to our air force crashed after taking off from Eskisehir for training purposes,” the ministry said in a statement on Tuesday. “The wreckage of the helicopter has been reached and search and rescue operations are continuing.”

The ministry did not specify the cause of the crash. Eskisehir is home to the air force’s 1st Main Jet Base Command.

Media footage showed emergency teams at the scene of the crash near Yorukakcayir village, about 15km (nine miles) west of Eskisehir city centre.

The AS-532 Cougar is a twin-engine, French-made multi-purpose helicopter that is used by militaries across the world.

On November 12, an army Sikorsky S-70 crashed near Malatya in southern Turkiye , killing four crew members. No official explanation has been given since.

Turkiye has the second-largest army in NATO.

articles.title: Meet Yash Patil, Indian-origin entrepreneur who took leave from Stanford to work with OpenAI, founded his own startup and then sold it for $4.5 billion
articles.summary: A 23-year-old Indian-origin entrepreneur who left Stanford University, joined OpenAI and later founded an artificial intelligence startup has struck a
articles.body: A 23-year-old Indian-origin entrepreneur who left Stanford University, joined OpenAI and later founded an artificial intelligence startup has struck a $4.5-billion acquisition deal barely 18 months after launching his company. Yash Patil, co-founder and chief executive of Applied Compute, has agreed to sell the startup to cybersecurity giant Palo Alto Networks in an all-stock transaction valued at $4.5 billion (around Rs 40,000 crore). The deal values the company at roughly $250 million for every month since it was founded.Patil founded Applied Compute in May 2025 with fellow former OpenAI employees Rhythm Garg and Linden Li. The startup helps companies customize, train and deploy artificial intelligence models using their own data, allowing businesses to build AI systems tailored to their needs rather than relying entirely on third-party models.The acquisition is expected to be completed in the third quarter of Palo Alto Networks' fiscal 2027, subject to regulatory approvals and other customary closing conditions.Following the acquisition, Patil is expected to become co-chief AI officer at Palo Alto Networks, alongside the Applied Compute team.From Stanford to OpenAIPatil grew up in Austin, Texas, in a family of Indian immigrants. He attended the Liberal Arts and Science Academy before studying computer science at Stanford University. His journey into AI reportedly began after a chance meeting with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman at a dinner hosted for Stanford engineering students.Following the launch of ChatGPT in 2022, Patil emailed Altman expressing interest in working on the chatbot. Altman encouraged him to apply for OpenAI's residency programme.Patil joined OpenAI in 2023 at the age of 20, taking a leave of absence from Stanford. He later worked as a technical staff member on post-training infrastructure, reasoning models and technology associated with Codex, OpenAI's AI coding assistant.At OpenAI, he met fellow Stanford alumni Rhythm Garg and Linden Li, who would later become his co-founders.The trio left OpenAI in 2025 to build Applied Compute, betting that companies would increasingly want to develop and operate their own AI systems using proprietary data.How Applied Compute became a billion-dollar startupThe idea for Applied Compute began taking shape in January 2025, around the time Chinese AI company DeepSeek released its R1 reasoning model, demonstrating the potential of powerful open-weight AI systems. The founders believed businesses would want to customize these models to suit their operations, train them using proprietary data and deploy them securely.The startup attracted major investors as it rapidly scaled.In June 2025, it raised $20 million in seed funding led by Benchmark, reportedly valuing the company at around $100 million. Another funding round brought in another $60 million, taking its valuation to approximately $500 million.By April 2026, Applied Compute had achieved unicorn status after raising $80 million at a $1.3-billion valuation in a funding round led by Kleiner Perkins.Earlier in November 2026, it raised $350 million at a valuation of $3.25 billion, in a round led by investor Elad Gil.The company said it had grown from zero revenue to more than $100 million in annualized revenue run-rate in just over 18 months, with a team of only a few dozen people.Its customers reportedly include Microsoft, Nvidia, DoorDash, Shopify, Harvey, Cognition, Mercor, Clay and Decagon.Why Palo Alto Networks is buying the startupPalo Alto Networks, one of the world's largest cybersecurity companies, has been expanding its AI capabilities as businesses increasingly deploy artificial intelligence in sensitive operations. Applied Compute's technology could help enterprises train and run customised AI models while incorporating security measures to protect data, systems and models against cyber threats. The acquisition is part of Palo Alto Networks' broader strategy to become a central player in the AI economy.CEO Nikesh Arora has said the company wants to position itself at the centre of AI adoption, particularly as enterprises increasingly require security infrastructure to support AI-powered operations. The $4.5-billion acquisition will bring Applied Compute's research team and platform into Palo Alto Networks, expanding its ability to help businesses deploy AI securely.You use AI every day. articles.title: Family of teen killed by Georgia police officer demands release of body camera footage
articles.summary: The family of a Black teenager in Georgia who was killed in a police shooting said Tuesday that it wants transparency and called on the police department to release the officer body camera footage.
articles.body: The family of a Black teenager in Georgia who was killed in a police shooting said Tuesday that it wants transparency and called on the police department to release the officer body camera footage. The 16-year-old, identified by the family and its attorneys as Tyrie Howse, was shot and killed Nov. 3 following an encounter with a Henry County police officer outside a Krispy Kreme in Stockbridge, about 21 miles southeast of Atlanta. Howse’s mother said Tuesday at a news conference that her son had left his cellphone somewhere the night before and went to get it. She was a few minutes from picking him up from the Krispy Kreme parking lot when he was shot, she said. “There was no reason, no reason at all for this to happen to him,” Taneshia Puckett said. Preliminary information released by the Georgia Bureau of Investigation said a Henry County police officer approached Howse and a 17-year-old in the parking lot of a Krispy Kreme, a news release states. The officer briefly spoke with the teens “before giving verbal commands for the 17-year-old to take his hands out of his pockets,” the release says. Authorities have not said what prompted the officer to approach the teens. The GBI said the 17-year-old “passed a handgun” to Howse, who allegedly ran away from the area with the gun, according to the release. “The 16-year-old did not drop the gun, and the officer shot at the 16-year-old, hitting him. Medical aid was provided to the 16-year-old. The 16-year-old was pronounced deceased on scene,” the GBI said. No officers were injured, and a firearm was recovered from the scene, according to the GBI. The officer involved in the shooting was placed on administrative leave pending the conclusion of the investigation, police said. Attorneys Ben Crump and Harry Daniels, who are representing Howse’s family, said they have viewed witness video showing the aftermath of the shooting and cannot see a firearm in the video they viewed. They called on officials to release the body camera footage. “There’s nothing stopping this Henry County Police Department or this Henry County district attorney from being transparent and showing the video,” Crump said at the news conference. He said Howse, a junior at Woodland High School, was an honor roll student who dreamed of becoming a pediatric nurse. “I fail to understand why the most dangerous thing in America to police seems to be young Black people running away from them,” he said. The Henry County Police Department said in a Nov. 10 statement that it asked the GBI to investigate the shooting and that it was aware of calls to release the body camera footage and other evidence, but “any potential release must be evaluated in coordination with the appropriate investigative and legal authorities.” The department did not immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday. The GBI said the investigative case file will be turned over to the Henry County District Attorney’s Office for review once completed. The district attorney’s office said in a Nov. 19 statement that it had not yet received the case file and was not in possession of the body camera footage. “Once the GBI completes its investigation and submits its findings, our office will conduct a thorough and independent review of the entire case file to determine whether criminal charges are warranted,” the district attorney’s office said. “Our decision will be guided solely by the facts, the evidence, and the applicable law.”

articles.title: Iran says 3 oil tankers hit underwater mines despite US naval escort
articles.summary: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) on Monday said three oil tankers escorted through the Strait of Hormuz were hit by underwater mines. The IRGC navy’s public relations office told the state-run Fars News Agency that one of the tankers was near the country’s southern coast while the other two were hit in the eastern…
articles.body:
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) on Monday said three oil tankers escorted through the Strait of Hormuz were hit by underwater mines.

The IRGC navy’s public relations office told the state-run Fars News Agency that one of the tankers was near the country’s southern coast while the other two were hit in the eastern part of the strait. The navy said the U.S. military air escort “failed to prevent the incidents.”

“Any transit through unauthorized routes or disregard for communicated warnings constitutes a violation and cooperation with the aggressor forces,” the IRGC said, adding that any alleged violations would be “dealt with firmly in accordance with previously announced regulations,” according to Fars News Agency.

The incident comes after the USS Theodore Roosevelt arrived in the Persian Gulf last week, joining the USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington aircraft carriers.

On Monday, the Treasury Department announced new sanctions on more than two dozen Iranian exchange houses, front companies and key personnel as part of “Operation Economic Outcast,” which has been the Trump administration’s attempt to cripple Iran’s economy since August.

“Iran’s economy is underwater, and its leaders are panicking,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement released Monday. “Iran’s shadow banking system is the last financial lifeline of a bankrupt regime. Treasury will continue dismantling these illicit networks until we have buried the head of the snake.”

Iranian strikes attacked three other tankers in or near the Strait of Hormuz last week, with two being hit while exiting the Persian Gulf through the strait. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Center said there were no casualties.

The U.S. and Iran have been locked in tit-for-tat strikes as both countries face pressure domestically to end the conflict. The Iranian strikes targeted a U.S. air base in Kuwait, while American forces struck Tehran’s Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday following an unofficial quiet period of roughly two months.

IRGC’s commander in chief, Maj. Gen. Ahmad Vahidi, warned on Tuesday that any future fighting between Iran and the U.S. may not be confined to the Middle East and could expand to other locations, if necessary, Fars News Agency reported .

President Trump said last week that the U.S. military was closely watching Pickaxe Mountain, a heavily fortified, deep underground Iranian nuclear and centrifuge-assembly complex located south of Natanz.

He warned Sunday that he was inclined to resume strikes against Iran after the new year if no deal is reached , though talks between both nations have been ongoing.

“All they do is talk, but it’s all bulls—. They’re more aggressive now than before the election,” Trump told Fox News on Sunday, referring to the 2026 midterm elections.

articles.title: Dalai Lama, office allotted bungalow in Lutyens' Delhi
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Centre has allotted a Type-7 government bungalow in Lutyens' Delhi to Tibetan spiritual leader the Dalai Lama and his office, Gaden
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Centre has allotted a Type-7 government bungalow in Lutyens' Delhi to Tibetan spiritual leader the Dalai Lama and his office, Gaden Phodrang, providing a permanent base for his visits to the national capital. Members of the Tibetan parliament-in-exile Tuesday described the move as a significant gesture of support towards the spiritual leader and the Tibetan community.Though housing and urban affairs ministry officials did not respond to queries, it is learnt that the ministry had transferred the bungalow on Pandit Ravi Shankar Shukla Lane to the ministry of external affairs last year after receiving a request. People aware of the development said usually, such transfers of accommodation are initially for three years and can be extended.According to news agency ANI, speaker of the Tibetan parliament-in-exile Dolma Tsering described the development as "very welcome news". She said the accommodation would make the Dalai Lama's visits to the national capital more convenient and provide greater comfort during his stay in Delhi.Welcoming the decision, Tibetan parliament-in-exile member and standing committee member Choedak Gyatso said, "government of India has given us refuge when we had no country. We lost our country, and it gave us Dharamshala when we had no land and gave us schools and many institutions that can preserve our culture."Recalling his recent official visit to Delhi, during which he met MPs, Gyatso said he had personally visited the bungalow along with the Tibetan deputy speaker and described the opportunity as a great honour.Gaden Phodrang, the Dalai Lama's office, was registered as a private trust in India in 2011 after he voluntarily relinquished political authority in favour of an elected Tibetan leadership. articles.title: Great British Bake Off winner crowned after high-stakes final
articles.summary: Judge Nigella Lawson describes the three finalists as "sensational" bakers.
articles.body:
Spoiler warning: This story reveals details of The Great British Bake Off final

Moyin Odeniran said he was "in shock" after being crowned the winner of the 17th series of The Great British Bake Off.

The 22-year-old from Loughton, Essex, described it as a "very busy time" as he juggled competing in the Channel 4 baking competition with completing his university studies .

Despite his dissertation being due a month after filming wrapped, Odeniran achieved a first in his political economy degree at King's College London.

He beat fellow finalists Tom Whittaker, from West Yorkshire, and Birmingham student Mo Mahir to the title in Tuesday night's episode.

"I don't know how that happened, I don't know how I got here. I can't believe it – I am in shock," the talented baker said.

"I have made friends for life and I have just loved every single second of it, and I don't think I could have asked for anything more."

Judge Paul Hollywood described Odeniran's efforts as "pure magic" after watching his jubilant celebrations with family and friends.

"He has done an amazing job because out of all the bakers he struggled at the beginning, and he actually got better and better," Hollywood said.

Fellow judge Nigella Lawson praised Odeniran as a "worthy winner", but also said the other finalists were "sensational".

The high-stakes final saw the three contestants tasked with making a citrus celebration cake, creme brulee donuts and a "spectacular tribute to iconic British landscapes".

Reflecting on his performance in the final, Odeniran said: "I didn't want to put too much pressure on myself, but I knew I had put my best foot forward.

"I couldn't have done anything better than I did and I had a great time doing it."

He said he got "quite exhausted" while filming the series and praised his mother, sister and close friends for their support.

"Earlier on, some of the challenges were quite difficult for me and I was shocked that I kept going through," Odeniran said.

"Before you get there you think you know how to bake, and by week two you question whether you know anything about baking."

He shared his gratitude at being able to learn from Lawson and Hollywood.

"I will never forget my time there and the friendships made which will always continue," the winner added.

Prior to the final, Odeniran told BBC Essex he planned to view it at a huge "watch party" at his local church .

articles.title: An 8-year-old girl waited for her mother who never arrived in 1987; nearly 40 years later, DNA evidence links a convicted killer to her disappearance, but her body remains missing
articles.summary: For nearly four decades, the disappearance of a Washington mother remained an unanswered question for her family.
articles.body: For nearly four decades, the disappearance of a Washington mother remained an unanswered question for her family. Wendy Aughe was 29 when she vanished in April 1987, leaving behind an eight-year-old daughter who had been waiting for her to arrive at a babysitter's home. Her body was never found, and investigators spent years trying to establish what had happened. The case remained unresolved until DNA evidence eventually linked a convicted murderer, already serving time in an Oregon prison, to evidence recovered from Aughe's bedroom. Now, almost 40 years after she disappeared, Darren Dee O'Neall has pleaded guilty to first-degree manslaughter in her death. He has received a 12-year prison sentence, but her remains have still not been recovered.Aughe's disappearance and the disturbing evidence found at her homeAs reported by The Bellingham Herald, Aughe was last seen on April 25, 1987, after spending time with a man she had met earlier that day. That man was Darren Dee O'Neall, who was 66 when he appeared in court in November 2026. According to court documents, the two had gone on a date, and O'Neall was subsequently seen driving Aughe's car without her.Concern grew when Aughe failed to collect her eight-year-old daughter from a babysitter. She was officially reported missing to Bellingham police on April 28, prompting officers to look into her disappearance. A visit to Aughe's home produced evidence that suggested something far more serious than an unexplained absence. The babysitter, accompanied by a police officer, went to the property to collect clothing for the child. Inside the bedroom, they discovered dried blood around the head of the bed. Investigators also found a semen stain on the bedsheet.Despite the evidence, the case did not immediately lead to a conviction for Aughe's disappearance. Her whereabouts remained unknown, while her family was left without an explanation for what had happened.DNA evidence brought investigators back to the caseA significant development came in August 2015, when the Washington State Patrol Crime Laboratory completed testing that connected O'Neall to the evidence collected from Aughe's bedroom. The laboratory confirmed a DNA match between O'Neall and the semen stain found on the bedsheet. Testing of a bloodstain on the upper-left corner of the bedsheet produced a partial DNA profile belonging to a single female. Investigators found that it matched Aughe's presumed DNA profile, according to court records.The findings gave investigators a direct forensic link to a man whose criminal history already included serious violent offences. Yet it would take several more years before he was formally charged in connection with Aughe's presumed death.On October 11, 2022, prosecutors charged O'Neall with her killing. The case was filed as second-degree murder, although he initially denied the charge. In March 2023, authorities brought him from Two Rivers Correctional Institution in Umatilla, Oregon, to Whatcom County, Washington, to face the proceedings.Earlier convictions put investigators on O'Neall's trailAughe's disappearance was not the first killing associated with O'Neall. In February 1989, he was convicted of first-degree murder in the death of Robin P. Smith, whose killing took place in Pierce County, Washington, in 1987. The circumstances of Smith's death were described as similar to those surrounding Aughe's disappearance, according to previous reporting by The Bellingham Herald. O'Neall was later convicted in August 1990 in a separate case involving a 14-year-old girl in Portland. He had kidnapped and repeatedly sexually assaulted the teenager in 1987. The conviction resulted in a 135-year prison sentence, as reported by The Bellingham Herald.His criminal record and suspected involvement in other violent offences also attracted attention from investigators in several states. Earlier reporting described him as a suspect in multiple killings and missing-person cases, and noted that he had once been among the FBI's Most Wanted.According to court records cited by The Bellingham Herald, O'Neall's earliest release date from the Oregon prison was May 2033.Nearly 40 years later, he admits responsibilityThe case finally reached a resolution of sorts in November 2026, when O'Neall appeared before a Whatcom County Superior Court judge. Rather than proceed with the original murder charge, he entered a guilty plea to an amended charge of first-degree manslaughter. The hearing attracted current and former Bellingham police officers, including detectives who had worked on the investigation, alongside members of Aughe's extended family.His lawyer, Peter Ramey, told the court that O'Neall wanted to acknowledge the suffering experienced by the family and accept responsibility. However, he also pointed out that a conviction at trial had not been certain, given the time that had passed since the alleged killing and the difficulties associated with prosecuting a case nearly four decades later. O'Neall did not make a personal statement during the hearing.Judge Robert Olson imposed the agreed sentence of 12 years in prison, followed by three years of community custody. The order also prohibits O'Neall from contacting Aughe's daughter, Charlina Johnson. The sentence was supported by Aughe's family and the Bellingham Police Department. Although the original charge carried the possibility of a more serious conviction, the manslaughter plea brought the long-running prosecution to an end.Daughters' family speaks of decades of loss and unanswered questionsFor Johnson, the hearing was about more than the outcome of a criminal case. She had spent most of her life without knowing what had happened to her mother, and the absence had shaped her childhood and adult years. She attended the sentencing carrying a framed photograph of Aughe taken shortly before she disappeared. The picture showed her mother around the time of Johnson's eighth birthday, just days before the two were separated. Johnson also brought a scrapbook assembled by her great-grandmother. It contained newspaper reports documenting the disappearance and the subsequent legal proceedings involving O'Neall.Addressing the judge, she spoke about the ordinary experiences she had missed, including the possibility of having her mother alongside her as she grew older and raised a family of her own. She also described the particular difficulty of living without a grave or a known resting place to visit.Her sister, Aughe's other daughter, died four years earlier, shortly after learning that O'Neall had been charged in connection with their mother's death. Johnson said she wished her sister could have been present for the sentencing. Her niece, Savannah Fields, also addressed the court, recalling the years her mother had spent trying to understand the disappearance and cope with the uncertainty surrounding Aughe's fate.Guilty plea brings legal closure, but Aughe's body remains missingDuring sentencing, Judge Olson referred to O'Neall's extensive record of violent offences and described his criminal history in particularly severe terms. The court ultimately accepted the jointly recommended punishment rather than proceeding to a trial. Speaking to The Bellingham Herald after the hearing, Johnson said she had been involved in discussions surrounding the plea agreement and already knew what sentence had been recommended. Hearing the decision formally delivered nevertheless brought a sense of relief. For her, the outcome meant she could begin moving forward without the same uncertainty about whether her mother's disappearance would ever be addressed in court.Disclaimer: This article is based on publicly available reports by The Bellingham Herald and other sources. articles.title: Israel raises prospect of preemptive strike over emerging Iranian chemical weapons threat
articles.summary: Israel Katz says Israel and the U.S. hold intelligence on Iran's alleged chemical weapons program, warning a preemptive strike remains possible.
articles.body: Israel accused Iran of developing chemical weapons Tuesday and raised the possibility of a preemptive strike to prevent Tehran from using them, warning that the regime seeks a strategic advantage after major setbacks in its war with Israel and the United States. Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz told reporters in Tel Aviv that Israel and the U.S. have intelligence indicating Iran began developing chemical weapons after their joint military campaign launched Feb. 28. Katz declined to disclose how far the program has progressed or where the weapons are being developed, though he noted Israeli intelligence has monitored Iran's effort for months and said that operational plans are in place. BLINKEN WARNS US GROUND INVASION OF IRAN WOULD BE 'ABSOLUTE DISASTER' AS TEHRAN ESCALATES ATTACKS "Iran is in the process of developing chemical weapons," Katz said, according to Israel's i24NEWS. "This intelligence information reached both the United States and Israel," he said. "Israel is determined not to allow Iran to acquire this kind of chemical weapons capability that would threaten the country and the entire region," he added. Katz described the program as a potentially game-changing threat to Israel and the broader Middle East, warning that the weapons could give Tehran leverage to rebuild its depleted military infrastructure, including its nuclear program. LIVE WWII-ERA GRENADES TURN UP IN UNLIKELY PLACE; BOMB SQUAD WARNS OF DANGER "They came out of the tunnels and saw what happened to them," Katz said of Iranian forces following the April ceasefire, according to comments reported by The Times of Israel. "They are looking for a weapon that gives them some balance against us. This process in Iran is new and comes in the wake of the damage they suffered. True, it is not nuclear, but it is still unconventional weapons." "If we thought this was already an unfolding event, we would act," Katz said. Katz also said that Israel must maintain the ability to act preemptively if intelligence shows an Iranian attack is imminent. "If the Iranians attack us first, it will be a failure," Katz said, according to Israel's Ynet news outlet. ISRAEL’S LEADING CONTENDER FOR PRIME MINISTER CLASHES WITH NETANYAHU OVER IRAN STRIKES The allegations come amid heightened U. S. intelligence concerns over Iranian threats against the American homeland. CNN reported Nov. 16, citing seven U. S. officials, that American intelligence indicated Iran was developing plans to potentially target senior Trump administration officials in Washington with a radiological "dirty bomb" or chemical weapon. Sources familiar with the intelligence described the planning as an effort to preserve potential retaliatory options rather than evidence of an imminent strike. The White House said at the time that it was monitoring potential threats but had identified no credible threats to the U.S. homeland. President Donald Trump subsequently warned that Iran would face severe consequences if it carried out such an attack. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi dismissed the reporting as "Iraq War-style propaganda" with "Israeli fingerprints all over it." articles.title: Todd Blanche declines to confirm if Nvidia’s Jensen Huang was investigated
articles.summary: The US attorney general refused to discuss claims by Donald Trump that his administration conducted a ‘thorough’ probe.
articles.body:
Amid bipartisan pushback over Nvidia’s decision to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang, United States Attorney General Todd Blanche has opted not to discuss whether the tech executive was under federal investigation.

At a press conference in Washington, DC, on Friday, Blanche was pressed by reporters over whether the Department of Justice had investigated Huang.

“What does that mean, ‘Had Huang been investigated’? For what?” Blanche responded.

“I don’t understand the question. Even the reporting from the various leaks or sources or whatever that was out there didn’t suggest that Huang himself was under some sort of investigation.”

Blanche also attempted to clarify US President Donald Trump’s comments that his administration had “exonerated” Huang of wrongdoing.

“What the president said is that he talked to a lot of people going into the decision that he made to encourage the board to reinstate him,” Blanche said. “And so, I’m not going to get into communications I had with the president about it, but what he was saying was true.”

Huang has been under scrutiny since late October, when The New York Times broke the story that he had been romantically involved with Alice Huang, an executive for the technology firm Megaspeed.

Alice Huang, according to the report, had been recruited by Chinese intelligence to help influence policy about US chip sales to China.

Under Jensen Huang’s leadership, Nvidia sold large quantities to Megaspeed, which allegedly diverted the semiconductor chips to China.

The New York Times cited anonymous US intelligence reports as its source. Beijing has denied the report as a “smear”.

Jensen Huang has since admitted to having extramarital affairs, including with a member of his staff, and on November 12, he resigned his leadership post.

But Trump, who has worked closely with Huang, petitioned for the disgraced CEO to regain control of Nvidia. Huang was reinstated on Monday.

In a social media post that day, Trump said the US “government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security”.

“The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct,” he wrote.

During an hour-long TV interview, also on Monday, the president said his administration had conducted a “thorough” investigation into Huang’s relationship with the alleged Chinese intelligence asset.

“We believe he’s fine. He’s absolutely fine,” Trump told CNBC. He added that he personally “convinced” Nvidia’s board to reinstate Huang.

That decision has sparked a political firestorm in Washington as Democrats and Republicans alike decried Trump’s involvement in Huang’s return, as well as the ongoing national security concerns.

The US and China are locked in a competition in the artificial intelligence (AI) sector, and for years, the US has restricted the sale of domestically made chips to the rival superpower, for fear that the technology could be stolen or appropriated by Beijing’s military.

Trump himself has investments in Nvidia. Since he began his second term as president, he has also struck a deal with Huang to give the US government a 15-percent cut of sales of certain AI chips to China, as part of a loosening of restrictions.

Those business deals spurred Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer to warn on Tuesday that Democrats would look into Trump’s arrangements with Nvidia.

“Senior Trump officials assured Nvidia that Huang posed no national security risk — a conclusion that would normally take months to thoroughly investigate — and provided no evidence to the public,” Schumer wrote in a statement . “Our committees will investigate.”

Democrats are set to take control of both chambers of Congress in the new year.

During Tuesday’s news conference, however, Blanche appeared to become defensive when questioned about how the Justice Department ensured Huang had not violated any US laws.

“I’m trying to be as transparent as I can be under the laws and rules around what we do,” Blanche said. “What I said last week is that we were looking into it.”

He continued by explaining that there were various types of “investigations”.

“The FBI, law enforcement looks into things all the time,” he said. “That doesn’t necessarily become a criminal investigation. Doesn’t necessarily become an indictment. It just literally is that. It’s looking into things”.

The attorney general said Trump was “free to talk about whatever he wants”, and he called Nvidia “a good corporate citizen”.

“Obviously, if Nvidia was the target, or was the subject of some criminal investigation, or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn’t be the message that the president is saying to the American people,” Blanche said.

articles.title: An Australian woman whose home was destroyed in a 2024 bushfire is rebuilding it with more than 350 earth-filled car tyres, glass bottles and aluminium cans
articles.summary: When a bushfire swept through Pomonal in western Victoria in 2024, Dee-Ann Kelly lost her home along with much of what she owned.
articles.body: When a bushfire swept through Pomonal in western Victoria in 2024, Dee-Ann Kelly lost her home along with much of what she owned. Two years later, she is rebuilding on the property, but the materials taking shape around her are far removed from those used in a conventional house. Her new home is being constructed with hundreds of discarded car tyres filled with earth, alongside glass bottles and aluminium cans. The unusual design, known as an Earthship, uses recycled materials and thick layers of earth to create an energy-efficient structure intended to offer greater protection against bushfires.How a Pomonal bushfire survivor turned rebuilding into a community effortAs reported by the ABC News, the February 2024 bushfire that struck Pomonal began after a dry lightning strike and spread rapidly through the area. By the time the fire had passed, 45 homes in the western Victorian town had been destroyed. Kelly managed to escape with her pets and a small number of belongings as the fire approached. The loss left her facing the task of starting again, but the support of people around her became part of the rebuilding process. Rather than opting for a standard construction project, she decided to create an Earthship, bringing together volunteers and people with experience in sustainable building.The work is being carried out under the supervision of a registered builder, with around 35 people travelling from different places to contribute. For Kelly, the construction has also become an opportunity to bring people together after the devastation caused by the fire. She described the first day of work as an especially memorable experience, with volunteers explaining what had brought them to the project. The community involvement, she said, had given the rebuilding effort a wider purpose beyond putting another house on the property.How discarded tyres are becoming part of the wallsReportedly, the structure is being built using more than 350 old car tyres, each packed tightly with earth to form sections of the walls. The tyres are being put to use as building components rather than being sent into the waste stream, where discarded tyres create an ongoing disposal challenge. Glass bottles and aluminium cans are also being incorporated into the construction. These materials become part of the wall system, while earth-based finishes are used to cover and complete the surfaces.The approach is associated with Earthship construction, a building method that makes use of reclaimed materials and natural resources. Martin Freney, who has designed and constructed around a dozen Earthship homes, is involved in the project. He explained that the method can reduce the need for conventional building products, including bricks, steel and timber.The construction also involves materials collected directly from the property. Volunteer Chevaun Buchecker, who travelled from South Australia to participate, helped prepare a natural wall finish using clay and sand sourced largely from the site. Straw is added to the mixture before it is used for plastering inside the house.Why the design is intended to offer bushfire protectionFire resilience is one of the main considerations behind Kelly's choice of building design. Earthships use substantial quantities of earth around their structures, creating a thick barrier between the living spaces and the outside environment. Freney said this construction method could make the buildings highly resistant to bushfires. The earth surrounding the structure acts as a protective layer, limiting the exposure of the house to external flames. The design is also intended to withstand other environmental conditions.The home is being built at ground level, although its finished appearance will be closer to that of an earth-covered or underground dwelling. Soil will be placed around and over much of the building, leaving the required openings and living areas exposed. However, the use of earth-packed tyres and recycled materials should not be taken as a guarantee that a building will survive every bushfire. Its performance depends on the complete design, construction standards and the conditions surrounding the property.Millions of discarded tyres find a new purpose in unconventional Earthship homesThe project also draws attention to the volume of discarded tyres generated in Australia each year. Millions are disposed of across the country, creating a challenge for waste management and recycling programmes. Using hundreds of them in a house offers an alternative application for material that would otherwise require disposal or processing. Freney said the approach also reduces demand for certain manufactured construction materials, since reclaimed items take the place of products that would ordinarily need to be produced and transported.The thick earth surrounding an Earthship has another purpose. It helps regulate indoor temperatures by providing insulation, reducing the need for conventional heating and cooling. The buildings are also designed to use energy and water efficiently, potentially lowering running costs over time.Despite its unconventional materials, the Pomonal house is not necessarily a cheaper construction project. Freney estimated that it would cost roughly the same as a conventional home, with the building expected to take about three months to complete.Volunteers help bring the Earthship togetherThe construction has attracted people from outside the local area, including volunteers who wanted to gain practical experience with alternative building techniques. Their involvement has extended from filling tyres and preparing wall materials to applying natural finishes.Buchecker said the people involved had arrived for different reasons, but the relationships formed during the work had become an important part of the experience. She travelled from South Australia specifically to take part in the build.The site has also developed its own informal features during construction, including a dog-shaped sculpture made from mud. Meanwhile, the roof has been attached as the building progresses towards completion.For Kelly, the project is closely connected to the future of Pomonal, a community where bushfire risk remains a part of life. She hopes the house will demonstrate that rebuilding in a fire-prone area can involve different construction choices, rather than simply reproducing the homes that existed before the disaster. She has said, "I'm wanting to create confidence in this community that you can live in a bushfire zone, you can build here and you can survive a bushfire.”You use AI every day. articles.title: Vatican releases Pope Francis' private diary detailing spiritual crisis, encounters with the devil
articles.summary: Pope Francis' private diary reveals a two-year spiritual crisis from 2021, with the late pontiff writing he felt tempted by the devil and saw hell in 2018.
articles.body: Excerpts from the late Pope Francis' private diary published Tuesday reveal that the pontiff endured a two-year spiritual crisis beginning in 2021, writing that he felt tempted by the devil and struggled with the weight of wielding power over the Catholic Church. The 160-page volume, "The Private Diary of Pope Francis," was compiled by Cardinal Victor Fernandez and spans entries from December 1992 through August 2024 — eight months before Francis died in April 2025 at age 88 — marking the first papal diary made public since the 1960s. In a December 2022 entry, Francis described his crisis as "all mixed with governance issues, pressure regarding decisions to make, and aridity and desolation," adding that he resisted becoming a leader "who uses others like puppets." "Last night I saw the entrance to Hell," he wrote in the 2018 entry. "I peeked in to look a little, and it terrified me. I grabbed the Rosary as a weapon. I thank the Lord for this help." Reacting Tuesday on "Varney & Co.," Fox News contributor and theologian Jonathan Morris said he was most struck not by the late pope's spiritual struggles, but by the Vatican's decision to publish them. articles.title: Kilmar Abrego Garcia is leaving the U.S. a ‘free man,’ Van Hollen says
articles.summary: Kilmar Abrego Garcia has been ordered by a federal judge to leave the United States by Tuesday, a U.S. official confirmed to NBC News.
articles.body: Kilmar Abrego Garcia has been ordered by a federal judge to leave the United States by Tuesday, a U.S. official confirmed to NBC News. In a statement Tuesday evening, Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Maryland, said Abrego Garcia is “traveling to a country of his choice, a free man — unharmed and with dignity.” The Salvadoran national became a central figure in the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown last year after he was mistakenly deported to his home country. The Washington Post reported earlier in the day that Abrego Garcia voluntarily agreed to leave the United States under an agreement with U.S. authorities who had sought his removal. The agreement, it said, would end those proceedings. Court records in Maryland have yet to reflect such an order. There have been a handful of sealed filings in his civil case against the administration over the past several weeks, however. The 31-year-old man immigrated to the U.S. illegally as a teenager, but has been in the United States for years, is married to an American, and has a child with her. He had lived and worked in Maryland for years under the regular supervision of Immigration and Customs Enforcement. In 2019, an immigration judge ruled that he could not be deported to El Salvador because he faced danger there from gang members. He was deported there anyway in 2025, but returned to the U.S. ICE officials admitted in court filings that his deportation there was an “administrative error.” Not long after his return to U.S., he was charged with human smuggling in a case stemming from a traffic stop in Tennessee in which he was driving a van with multiple immigrant passengers. Tennessee did not prosecute him. A federal judge dismissed the case, saying the Trump administration failed to rebut the “presumption of vindictiveness.” The government appealed. The administration continued to pursue Abrego’s removal, and he was fighting that in a lawsuit that was ongoing prior to today’s news. Abrego Garcia has been fighting deportation to Liberia, as proposed by Department of Homeland Security officials. He wanted to go to Costa Rica, according to court records. President Donald Trump and immigration officials alleged Abrego Garcia was an MS-13 gang member, something he denied.

articles.title: CIA hit by cyberattack amid string of US government system disruptions: Report
articles.summary: An unclassified Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) system used to handle open-source intelligence was breached in a cyberattack, but no classified
articles.body: An unclassified Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) system used to handle open-source intelligence was breached in a cyberattack, but no classified information was compromised, and the issue has since been resolved, The Associated Press reported citing sources familiar with the incident. The breach came to light on Tuesday, amid a series of recent technical failures and suspected cyber incidents affecting key US government agencies and major companies.The affected system handled open-source intelligence, the report said, citing an anonymous source. The person was not authorised to speak publicly about the matter.What was affectedThe compromised system was used to collect and analyse publicly available information. This includes data from the internet, commercial satellites and private data brokers.Although such information is generally public or semi-public, it can provide intelligence analysts with significant insights. Analysts can also combine it with information gathered through classified intelligence operations to build a more detailed picture.It was not immediately clear what specific information was compromised or who was responsible for the breach.The New York Times first reported the incident on Tuesday.CIA breach follows series of US system disruptionsThe incident comes after several technical failures and suspected cyber incidents raised concerns about the security of US government systems and critical infrastructure.An internal network used by the National Security Agency (NSA) to communicate classified information was offline for some time last week. The FBI is also investigating an apparent breach of a national law enforcement database maintained by the agency.These incidents followed a nationwide ground stop that disrupted air travel after air traffic controllers struggled to communicate with pilots.Several major companies, including Apple, JPMorgan Chase and Microsoft, also experienced system outages this month.The disruptions have raised questions about vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure, banking systems and digital services used by millions of people.Trump administration denies coordinated cyberattackThe Donald Trump administration has said the recent outages were not part of a coordinated cyberattack.Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton appeared on Sunday morning news programmes to reassure Americans following the disruptions.Clayton said the outages were largely linked to efforts to patch and upgrade systems to stay ahead of hackers. articles.summary: Donald Trump's administration is reportedly weighing strikes on Iran's senior leaders, including Mojtaba Khamenei, as the war nears its ninth month.
articles.body: The Trump administration has renewed internal discussions about potentially targeting senior Iranian regime leaders in strikes that some officials believe could end the ongoing war, according to reports. Citing a U. S. official and another source, NBC News reported Tuesday that some officials believe eliminating senior figures could pressure Tehran to end the conflict by showing that Washington can locate and strike the regime's leadership at any time. Though the option has long been under consideration, it has "been under renewed discussion in recent weeks" as President Donald Trump deliberates over the next phase of the war, two sources told the outlet. The deliberations come amid reports that Iran could be developing a radioactive "dirty bomb" and a report citing U. S. intelligence assessments of potential Iranian plots involving chemical weapons aimed at senior officials in Washington. We know who they are, where they are. We'll find out about it. We will not allow that," Trump had told reporters at the White House Nov. 20. Iran's surviving leadership includes Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who succeeded his father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, after the elder Khamenei was killed in the opening strikes of the war Feb. 28. Other senior figures in Iran's military and national security apparatus include Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Commander Ahmad Vahidi, armed forces chief of staff Ali Abdollahi, army chief Amir Hatami and Mohsen Rezaei, a former IRGC commander in chief reportedly appointed secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council in August 2026. AFTER 6 MONTHS OF WAR, US MUST PREPARE FOR A FUTURE AFTER IRAN’S GOVERNMENT FALLS NBC News did not identify any of those officials as specific targets of the operations under discussion. Administration officials opposed to the proposal have reportedly warned that targeting Iranian leaders could expose American officials to retaliatory attacks, stiffen the resolve of surviving regime figures and undermine future diplomatic efforts to end the conflict, now in its ninth month. The administration continues to weigh military options, enforce its naval blockade and assert control over the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz. The debate comes months after U. S. and Israeli strikes killed Iran's supreme leader and other senior military and intelligence officials, igniting a prolonged conflict centered on Tehran's nuclear program, ballistic missile capabilities and regional military activities. Mojtaba Khamenei, who was reportedly injured in the strikes that killed his father, has not been seen publicly since assuming power, though he has warned Washington and Jerusalem against resuming major attacks on Iranian leadership. The warning reportedly followed a meeting with senior Iranian military commanders, including Abdollahi, Hatami and Vahidi. On Oct. 31, Khamenei also directed Iran's armed forces to prepare an "immediate, impactful and geographically unrestricted response" to any future threats.
